<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
The Artin--Davenport conjecture is true.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
Let $X\subset\operatorname{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$ be a cubic
hypersurface defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ which is not a cone, with $n\geqslant 5$ and 
singular locus which is empty or of codimension at least $4$ in $X$.
Then the Hasse principle holds for $X$.
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:sing}
Let $n\geqslant 2$ and let  $X\subset\operatorname{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$ be a cubic
hypersurface defined over $\mathbb{Q}$,  
with  singular locus of 
 codimension at most $\lfloor (n-1)/3 \rfloor$ in $X$.
Then $X(\mathbb{Q}) \ne \emptyset$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:Fq}
Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field of order $q$ and
let $X\subset \operatorname{\mathbb{P}}^{N}$ be a geometrically integral cubic hypersurface defined over $\mathbb{F}_q$,
where $N\geqslant 2$.
If $\sigma=\dim \operatorname{Sing}(X)\in \{-1,\dots,N-2\}$, where $\operatorname{Sing}(X)$ is the singular locus of $X$, then
\begin{equation*}
\#X(\mathbb{F}_q)-\frac{q^N-1}{q-1}
\ll_N q^{(N+\sigma)/2}.
\end{equation*}
Moreover,
$$
\#X(\mathbb{F}_q)-\frac{q^N-1}{q-1}\ll_N
\begin{cases}
q^{N-2} & \text{ if $N\geqslant 3$ and $X$ is not a cone,}\\
q^{N-3/2} &\text{ otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The first result can be extracted from
Theorem~1 of \cite{Hoo91}.
The second is the main result of 
\cite{Bro13} and the last follows from the  Lang--Weil estimate \cite{LW}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
Although Lemma~\ref{lem:Fq} will suffice for the present paper, 
it might be possible to obtain sharper results for $N\geqslant 4$
by using \cite[Theorem~5.5]{Wan23}.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{Bro-integral-cone}
Let $N\geqslant 3$.
If $X \subset \operatorname{\mathbb{P}}^N_\mathbb{Q}$ is a cubic hypersurface
with $X(\mathbb{Q}) = \emptyset$,
then $X$ is geometrically integral and is not a cone.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
\label{field-of-maximal-vertex}
It will be useful to know how to compute the
maximal vertex of a conical cubic hypersurface.
If $C(\bm{y})$ is a cubic form in $N$ variables
over a perfect field $K$,
then its maximal vertex over $\overline{K}$
coincides with the base change of its maximal vertex over $K$.
This follows from Galois descent,
since the maximal vertex over a field $L/K$ corresponds to the $L$-vector space
\[
M(L) = \{\bm{z}\in L^N: C(\bm{y}+t\bm{z}) - C(\bm{y}) = 0\in L[\bm{y},t]\},
\]
which satisfies $M(\overline{K})^{\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)} = M(K)$.
This is particularly clean if $K$ has characteristic $\neq 2,3$,
in which case by Taylor expansion the condition in $M(L)$
is equivalent to $H_C(\bm{z})=\bm{0}$.
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{Thm: ZaksBoundSingLocus}
Let $Y\subset \operatorname{\mathbb{P}}^N$ be a geometrically integral hypersurface of degree $\geqslant 2$ over a field.
Let $H\subset \operatorname{\mathbb{P}}^N$ be a hyperplane.
Then $\dim \operatorname{Sing}(Y\cap H)\leqslant \dim\operatorname{Sing}(Y)+1$.
In particular, if $\dim Y - \dim\operatorname{Sing}(Y) \geqslant 4$,
then $Y\cap H$ is geometrically integral.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
This follows from Zak's bound
recorded in Theorem~2 of Katz's appendix to \cite{Hoo91}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{Le: NoetherNormalisation}
Let $Y\subset\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}_\mathbb{Z}^N$ be a closed subscheme whose
generic fibre $Y_{\mathbb{Q}}\subset\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}_\mathbb{Q}^N$
has dimension $0\leqslant d\leqslant N-1$.
Let $\pi\colon \operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^N \to \operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^d$ be the projection onto the first $d$ coordinates.
There exist
a matrix $A \in \operatorname{Mat}_{N\times N}(\mathbb{Z}) \cap \operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb{Q})$,
an integer $C\geqslant 1$,
and polynomials $F_j\in \mathbb{Z}[x_1,\dots,x_d,x_{d+j}]$ for $1\leqslant j\leqslant N-d$,
such that the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The composite map
$Y_{\mathbb{Q}} \xrightarrow{A} \operatorname{\mathbb{A}}_\mathbb{Q}^N \xrightarrow{\pi} \operatorname{\mathbb{A}}_\mathbb{Q}^d$
is finite.

\item For each $1\leqslant j\leqslant N-d$,
we have $F_j = Cx_{d+j}^C + O_{x_1,\dots,x_d}(x_{d+j}^{C-1})$,
and the polynomial $F_j(A\bm{x})\in \mathbb{Z}[\bm{x}]=\mathbb{Z}[x_1,\dots,x_N]$
vanishes on $Y$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Since the field $\mathbb{Q}$ is infinite,
it is a well-known consequence of
Noether normalisation
that there exists a dense open subvariety $U \subset \operatorname{GL}_N$ over $\mathbb{Q}$
such that (1) holds for all $A\in U(\mathbb{Q})$,
as remarked in \cite[p.~284]{Eis95}.
Since $\operatorname{Mat}_{N\times N}(\mathbb{Z}) \cap \operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb{Q})$ is Zariski dense in $\operatorname{GL}_N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$,
we can satisfy (1) with a matrix $A\in \operatorname{Mat}_{N\times N}(\mathbb{Z}) \cap \operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb{Q})$.
It follows from (1) that each $x_{d+j}$ satisfies a monic non-constant polynomial relation in $\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\dots,x_d][x_{d+j}]$ on the variety $A(Y_{\mathbb{Q}})$.
After multiplying each relation by a suitable monomial in $x_{d+j}$, 
we are led to (2),
since every element of the ideal $I(Y_{\mathbb{Q}}) = I(Y) \otimes \mathbb{Q}$
is a nonzero rational scalar times an element of $I(Y)$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{LEM:basically-zippel}
Let $Y\subset\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}_\mathbb{Z}^N$ be a closed subscheme whose
generic fibre
has dimension $0\leqslant d\leqslant N$.
Let $m\geqslant1$ be an integer.
Let $\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^N$,
$L\geqslant1$ and $\bm{v}_0\in\mathbb{R}^N$.
Then
\begin{equation*}
\#\{\bm{v}\in Y(\mathbb{Z}):|\bm{v}-\bm{v}_0|\leqslant L,\ 
\bm{v}\equiv\bm{b}\bmod m\}
\ll_Y (1+L/m)^d.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
This is trivial if $d=N$.
If $d\leqslant N-1$, use Lemma~\ref{Le: NoetherNormalisation}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{Le: StratGeoSieveStep1}
Let $Y\subset\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}_\mathbb{Z}^N$ be a closed subscheme whose
generic fibre
has dimension at most $d$,
where $0\leqslant d\leqslant N$.
Let $m\geqslant1$ be an integer.
Let $\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^N$,
$L\geqslant1$ and $\bm{v}_0\in\mathbb{R}^N$.
If $S \gg 1 + L/m$, then
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{\substack{q\sim S \\
\gcd(q,m)=1}}
\sum_{\substack{\bm{v}\in \mathbb{Z}^N \setminus Y(\mathbb{Z}) \\
|\bm{v}-\bm{v}_0|\leqslant L \\
\bm{v}\equiv\bm{b}\bmod m \\
\bm{v}\bmod q\in Y(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})}}
\mu^2(q)
\ll_{Y,\varepsilon} (LS+|\bm{v}_0|)^\varepsilon (1 + L/m)^{d+1}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Since the ideal $I(Y)$ is finitely generated,
the divisor bound on a suitable polynomial in $I(Y)$
for each vector $\bm{v}\in \mathbb{Z}^N \setminus Y(\mathbb{Z})$
implies that
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{\substack{q\sim S \\
\gcd(q,m)=1}}
\sum_{\substack{\bm{v}\in \mathbb{Z}^N \setminus Y(\mathbb{Z}) \\
|\bm{v}-\bm{v}_0|\leqslant L \\
\bm{v}\equiv\bm{b}\bmod m \\
\bm{v}\bmod q\in Y(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})}}
\mu^2(q)
\ll_{Y,\varepsilon}
\sum_{\substack{\textnormal{admissible }\bm{v}\in \mathbb{Z}^N \setminus Y(\mathbb{Z}) \\
|\bm{v}-\bm{v}_0|\leqslant L \\
\bm{v}\equiv\bm{b}\bmod m}} (L+|\bm{v}_0|)^\varepsilon,
\end{equation*}
where we call a vector $\bm{v}\in \mathbb{Z}^N$
admissible if there exists a square-free integer $q\sim S$
with $\gcd(q,m)=1$
such that $\bm{v}\bmod q\in Y(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})$.
Lemma~\ref{Le: StratGeoSieveStep1} will follow if we can prove that
\begin{equation}
\label{n10:translated-composite-sieve}
f(Y) := \sum_{\substack{\textnormal{admissible }\bm{v}\in \mathbb{Z}^N \\
|\bm{v}-\bm{v}_0|\leqslant L \\
\bm{v}\equiv\bm{b}\bmod m}} 1
\ll_{Y,\varepsilon} (LS+|\bm{v}_0|)^\varepsilon (1 + L/m)^{d+1}.
\end{equation}
We include vectors $\bm{v}\in Y(\mathbb{Z})$ in \eqref{n10:translated-composite-sieve}
so that $f(Y)$ is monotone, in the sense that if $Y \subset Y'$ then $f(Y) \leqslant f(Y')$.
The inequality \eqref{n10:translated-composite-sieve}
is trivial if $d=N$, so suppose that $d\leqslant N-1$.
We may assume $\dim Y_\mathbb{Q} = d$,
by adding a linear space of generic dimension $d$
to $Y$ if necessary.
After changing variables as in Lemma~\ref{Le: NoetherNormalisation},
and further enlarging $Y$ if necessary,
we may assume in \eqref{n10:translated-composite-sieve}
that $Y$ is the simultaneous zero locus
of integer polynomials of the form
$$F_j(x_1,\dots,x_d,x_{d+j}) = Cx_{d+j}^C + O_{x_1,\dots,x_d}(x_{d+j}^{C-1}),$$
for $1\leqslant j\leqslant N-d$,
where $C\geqslant 1$.
The contribution of $\bm{v}\in Y(\mathbb{Z})$ to the left-hand side of
\eqref{n10:translated-composite-sieve}
is negligible by Lemma~\ref{LEM:basically-zippel}.
If $\bm{v}\notin Y(\mathbb{Z})$, then let $j_*$ be the minimal index $j$
for which $F_j(v_1,\dots,v_d,v_{d+j}) \ne 0$.
Once $v_1,\dots,v_d,v_{d+j_*}$ are chosen,
there are
$O_{Y,\varepsilon}((L+|\bm{v}_0|)^\varepsilon)$ choices for $q\mid F_{j_*}(v_1,\dots,v_d,v_{d+j_*})$,
by the divisor bound.
For each $j\ne j_*$, the congruence $F_j(v_1,\dots,v_d,y_{d+j}) \equiv 0\bmod{q}$
has at most $\gcd(C,q) C^{\omega(q)}=O(q^\varepsilon)$ solutions $y_{d+j}\bmod{q}$,
by the Chinese remainder theorem.
Each residue $y_{d+j}\bmod{q}$ has $O(1 + L/(qm)) = O(1)$
integral lifts $v_{d+j}$ satisfying
$v_{d+j}\equiv y_{d+j}\bmod q$ and
$v_{d+j}\equiv b_{d+j}\bmod m$,
since $\gcd(q,m)=1$ and $q\sim S \gg L/m$.
Thus the contribution to \eqref{n10:translated-composite-sieve}
from the index $j_*$
is $$\ll_{Y,\varepsilon} \sum_{v_1,\dots,v_d,v_{d+j_*}} (L+|\bm{v}_0|)^\varepsilon S^\varepsilon
\ll_\varepsilon (LS+|\bm{v}_0|)^{2\varepsilon} (1+L/m)^{d+1}.$$
Summing over $1\leqslant j_*\leqslant N-d$ completes the proof of \eqref{n10:translated-composite-sieve}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:stratified-composite-sieve}
Let $Y_0,Y_1,\ldots,Y_s\subset\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}_\mathbb{Z}^N$ be closed subschemes
whose generic fibres have dimensions at most $d_0,d_1,\dots,d_s$,
respectively.
Suppose that
\[
 N\geqslant d_0\geqslant d_1\geqslant\cdots\geqslant d_s\geqslant0.
\]
Let $\mathcal U \subset Y_0(\mathbb{Z})$ and $0 \leqslant \alpha \leqslant d_0$.
Suppose that
uniformly over $\bm{v}_0\in \mathbb{R}^N$,
$L\geqslant 1$,
$\bm{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^N$
and integers $q\geqslant 1$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:stratified-progression-hypothesis}
\#\{\bm{v}\in \mathcal U:
|\bm{v}-\bm{v}_0|\leqslant L,\;
\bm{v}\equiv\bm{a}\bmod q\}
\ll_{\mathcal U,\varepsilon}
(L+|\bm{v}_0|)^\varepsilon (1+L/q)^\alpha.
\end{equation}
Let $m\geqslant 1$ be an integer.
Let $\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^N$,
$L\geqslant1$ and $\bm{v}_0\in\mathbb{R}^N$.
Let
$${\textstyle \mathcal C
:= \left\{\bm{v}\in \mathcal U \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^s Y_i(\mathbb{Z}):
|\bm{v}-\bm{v}_0|\leqslant L,\;
\bm{v}\equiv\bm{b}\bmod m\right\}.}$$
For $R_1,\ldots,R_s \geqslant 1/2$, let
\[
\mathcal N(\bm R)
:= \sum_{\substack{q_i\sim R_i \\
\gcd(q_i,q_j)=1\ (i\ne j) \\ \gcd(q_i,m)=1}}
\sum_{\bm{v}\in\mathcal C}
\prod_{i=1}^s \mu^2(q_i)
\bm1_{\bm{v}\bmod q_i\in Y_i(\mathbb{Z}/q_i\mathbb{Z})}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stratified-composite-sieve}
\mathcal N(\bm R)
\ll_{\mathcal U,Y_0,\dots,Y_s,\alpha,\varepsilon}
(LR_1\cdots R_s + |\bm{v}_0|)^\varepsilon
\left(1
+ \frac{(L/m)^\alpha}{\prod_{i=1}^s R_i^{\alpha-d_i-1}}
+ \sum_{j=1}^s \frac{(L/m)^{d_j+1}}{\prod_{i=j+1}^s R_i^{d_j-d_i}}
\right),
\end{equation}
where empty products are interpreted as $1$.
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The contribution to $\mathcal N(\bm R)$
from any individual vector $\bm{v}\in\mathcal C$
is $\ll (L+|\bm{v}_0|)^\varepsilon$,
by the divisor bound.
Thus \eqref{eq:stratified-composite-sieve} is trivial if $L \leqslant m$.
We may therefore assume $L>m$.

By the Lang--Weil bound,
we have $\#Y_i(\mathbb{F}_p) \ll p^{d_i}$ for all $p$.
If $R_1\cdots R_s\leqslant L/m$,
then there are $\ll \prod_i q_i^{d_i+\varepsilon}$
available residue classes $\bm{v}\bmod{q_1\cdots q_s}$.
Applying \eqref{eq:stratified-progression-hypothesis}
with $q = mq_1\cdots q_s \ll L$ gives
\begin{equation*}
\frac{\mathcal N(\bm R)}{(LR_1\cdots R_s + |\bm{v}_0|)^\varepsilon}
\ll \sum_{q_i\sim R_i}
(L/q)^\alpha
\prod_i q_i^{d_i}
\ll \frac{(L/m)^\alpha}{\prod_{i=1}^s R_i^{\alpha-d_i-1}},
\end{equation*}
which is satisfactory.
If $R_1\cdots R_s > L/m$, choose $1\leqslant j\leqslant s$ such that
\[
R_{j+1}\cdots R_s \ll L/m \ll R_jR_{j+1}\cdots R_s.
\]
This is possible because $R_1,\dots,R_s \gg 1$ and $1 \ll L/m \ll R_1\cdots R_s$.
Given $\bm{v}$, the number of available moduli $q_i$
is $\ll (L+|\bm{v}_0|)^\varepsilon$ for each $i<j$,
by the divisor bound.
On the other hand, there are $\ll \prod_{i>j} q_i^{d_i+\varepsilon}$
available residue classes $\bm{v}\bmod{\prod_{i>j} q_i}$.
Lemma~\ref{Le: StratGeoSieveStep1},
with $M := m\prod_{i>j} q_i \gg L/R_j$ in place of $m$,
with $Y := Y_j$ and with $S := R_j \gg 1 + L/M$, gives
\begin{equation*}
\frac{\mathcal N(\bm R)}{(LR_1\cdots R_s + |\bm{v}_0|)^\varepsilon}
\ll \sum_{q_i\sim R_i\ (i>j)} (1+L/M)^{d_j+1}
\prod_{i>j} q_i^{d_i}
\ll \sum_{q_i\sim R_i\ (i>j)} (L/M)^{d_j+1}
\prod_{i>j} q_i^{d_i}
\end{equation*}
since $L/M \gg 1$.
This is $\ll (L/m)^{d_j+1} \prod_{i>j} R_i^{d_i-d_j}$, which is satisfactory.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:Iq'}
Let $w(\bm{x})=\omega((\bm{x}_0-\bm{x})/\ell)$, where
$\omega\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is supported on $[-1,1]^n$,
and $\ell>0$ and $\bm{x}_0\in\mathbb{R}^n$ are fixed.
Let $\varepsilon>0$ and let $N\geqslant 1$.
Assume $1\leqslant q\leqslant P^2$ and $|\theta| \leqslant q^{-1}P^{-1}$.
Then we have
$$
I(\theta;q^{-1}\bm{v})
\ll_{F,\varepsilon,N} |\bm{v}|^{-N},
$$
if $|\bm{v}|\gg P^3$. Alternatively, when
$|\bm{v}|\ll P^3$, we have
$$
I(\theta;q^{-1}\bm{v})
\ll_{F,\varepsilon,N}
P^{-N}+\operatorname{Vol}\left\{\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n:
|\bm{x}/P-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant 2\ell,\;
|q\theta\nabla F(\bm{x})-\bm{v}|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0
\right\},
$$
where $V_0=qP^{-1}\max\{1,\sqrt{|\theta|P^3}\}$.
Finally, we have
$$
I(\theta;q^{-1}\bm{v})
\ll_{F,\varepsilon,N} P^{-N},
$$
if $|\bm{v}|\geqslant P^{2\varepsilon}qP^{-1}\max\{1,|\theta|P^3\}$.
The implied constants above may depend on $\omega$, $\ell$ and $\bm{x}_0$
in addition to $F,\varepsilon,N$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
We may assume that $P$ is sufficiently large, the bounded $P$ case
following from the trivial bound and integration by parts.
The first two parts directly follow from  taking $g=F$ and $H=O(1)$ in
\cite[Lemma~9 and its proof]{41}.
(Although \cite[Lemma~9]{41} is written without the condition $|\bm{x}/P-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant 2\ell$,
it is clear from the proof that we may include it, since $w(\bm{x}/P)$
is supported on the strictly smaller box $|\bm{x}/P-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant \ell$.)
For the final part, it suffices to show that the volume is over the empty  set in the second estimate 
for $I(\theta;q^{-1}\bm{v})$,  
if $|\bm{v}|\geqslant P^{2\varepsilon} qP^{-1} \max\left\{1,|\theta |P^3\right\}$. 
Note that $q\theta \nabla F(\bm{x})\ll q|\theta|P^2$ if $|\bm{x}/P-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant 2\ell$.  If 
$|\theta |P^3<1$, then the claim is obvious.  
If $|\theta |P^3\geqslant 1$, then the claim is also clear, since  then 
$|\bm{v}|\geqslant P^{2\varepsilon} qP^{-1}\cdot |\theta |P^3=q |\theta |P^{2+2\varepsilon}\gg q |\theta |P^{2}$, which would imply the contradictory upper bound
$|\bm{v}|\ll P^\varepsilon V_0 = P^\varepsilon  qP^{-1} \sqrt{|\theta |P^3}$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{LEM:dav-bad-tangent-space}
Let $0\leqslant r\leqslant n$.
Put $V_{-1}:=\emptyset$.
If $\bm{x}\in V_r \setminus V_{r-1}$,
$\bm{v}\in T_{\bm{x}}V_r$,
and $\bm{y},\bm{z}\in\ker H(\bm{x})$,
then $$\bm{y}^tH(\bm{v})\bm{z}=0.$$
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
If $r=n$, the claim is trivial. If $r=0$, then $V_0$ is a
linear space, so $\bm{v}\in V_0$ and $H(\bm{v})=0$.
Thus assume $0<r<n$.
After a linear change of variables, we may suppose that
$$
H(\bm{x})=
\begin{pmatrix}
M&0\\
0&0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \det M\ne0,
$$
where $M$ is an $r\times r$ matrix.
For $i,j>r$, let $\Delta_{ij}(\bm{w})$ be the minor of $H(\bm{w})$
formed from rows $1,\dots,r,i$ and columns $1,\dots,r,j$.
Since $\Delta_{ij}$ vanishes on $V_r$ and
$\bm{v}\in T_{\bm{x}}V_r$, its differential at $\bm{x}$ annihilates
$\bm{v}$. On the other hand, linearity of $H$ gives
$$
\Delta_{ij}(\bm{x}+\varepsilon\bm{v})
\equiv \varepsilon\det(M)H(\bm{v})_{ij}\pmod{\varepsilon^2}.
$$
Hence $H(\bm{v})_{ij}=0$ for all $i,j>r$.
Since $\bm{y},\bm{z}\in\ker H(\bm{x})$ have their first $r$
coordinates zero, this proves $\bm{y}^tH(\bm{v})\bm{z}=0$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
Let us briefly sketch a
more conceptual,
but less elementary,
proof of Lemma~\ref{LEM:dav-bad-tangent-space}.
By general machinery or explicit calculation,
the vector spaces $\ker H(\bm{x})$
form a vector bundle over $\bm{x}\in V_r \setminus V_{r-1}$.
Let $\boldsymbol{\zeta}(\bm{w})$ be a local section extending $\bm{z}$ for $\bm{w}$ in a sufficiently small neighbourhood of $\bm{x}$, with
$H(\bm{w})\boldsymbol{\zeta}(\bm{w})=\bm0$
and $\boldsymbol{\zeta}(\bm{x})=\bm{z}$.
K\"{a}hler differentiation at $\bm{x}$ in the direction $\bm{v}$,
using the product rule, gives $H(\bm{v})\bm{z}+H(\bm{x})d\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{\bm{x}}(\bm{v})=\bm0$.
Multiplying by $\bm{y}^t$ gives $\bm{y}^tH(\bm{v})\bm{z}=0$,
since $\bm{y}^tH(\bm{x})=0$.
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- defin-1: body_md -->
\label{defn : good}
We say that the cubic form $F$ is {\em good} if
for any $H \geqslant 1$ and any $\varepsilon>0$ we have the upper bound   
\[
\#\{\bm{z}\in\mathbb{Z}^n: |\bm{z}|\leqslant H,~ \operatorname{rank}(H(\bm{z}))=r\}
\ll_{F,\varepsilon} H^{r+\varepsilon},
\]
for each $0\leqslant r\leqslant n$,
where the implied constant only depends on $F$ and $\varepsilon$.
<!-- end defin-1 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{LEM:my-guy-slop}
Assume $X(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$.
If $n\geqslant 2$, then $r(F) \geqslant 2 \lceil n/3 \rceil$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Since $X(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$, the polynomial $F$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.
It follows from Zak \cite[Proposition~4.2 and Corollary~4.4]{myguyzak} (with $N'=n-1$)
that
\begin{equation}
\label{EQ:my-guy-zak}
\det H \equiv 0\bmod{F^{n-r(F)}}.
\end{equation}
For completeness, let us unravel Zak's proof of \eqref{EQ:my-guy-zak}.
If $r(F)=n$, then \eqref{EQ:my-guy-zak} is trivial,
so assume $r(F)<n$.
By definition of $r(F)$,
every $(r(F)+1)\times(r(F)+1)$ minor of $H$
is divisible by $F$.
The divisibility \eqref{EQ:my-guy-zak} then
follows from \cite[Proposition~4.3]{myguyzak},
an elementary result on matrices,
applied to the matrix $H$
over the integral domain $A = \mathbb{Q}[\bm{x}]$,
with principal prime ideal $\mathfrak p = (F)$.

Since $\det H \ne 0$ by goodness (Definition~\ref{defn : good}),
comparing degrees in \eqref{EQ:my-guy-zak}
gives $n \geqslant 3(n-r(F))$ and hence $r(F)\geqslant 2n/3$.
If $n\equiv 0\bmod{3}$ then $r(F) \geqslant 2n/3 = 2\lceil n/3\rceil$,
and if $n\equiv 2\bmod{3}$ then $r(F) \geqslant \lceil 2n/3 \rceil = (2n+2)/3 = 2\lceil n/3\rceil$.
It remains to prove Lemma~\ref{LEM:my-guy-slop} when $n\equiv 1\bmod{3}$.
In this case, $r(F) \geqslant \lceil 2n/3 \rceil = (2n+1)/3$,
whereas $2\lceil n/3\rceil = (2n+4)/3$.
Assume for contradiction that $r(F) = (2n+1)/3$.
Then $n-r(F) = (n-1)/3$, so \eqref{EQ:my-guy-zak} gives
\begin{equation*}
\det H = F^{(n-1)/3} L
\end{equation*}
for some nonzero linear form $L\in \mathbb{Q}[\bm{x}]$,
since $\deg(\det H) = n$.
Let
\begin{equation*}
M := \{\bm{x}\in \operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n: L(\bm{x})=0\}
\cong \operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^{n-1}.
\end{equation*}
Then $\dim M = n-1 \geqslant 1$, so $M(\mathbb{Q}) \setminus \{\bm0\}$ is Zariski dense in $M$.
If $M$ is contained in $V_s$ but not in $V_{s-1}$,
then it follows that $M(\mathbb{Q}) \setminus \{\bm0\}$ is contained in $V_s$ but not in $V_{s-1}$.
Here $s<n$, since $M \subset \{\bm{x}\in \operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n: \det H(\bm{x})=0\}$.
Choose a vector $\bm{x}\in M(\mathbb{Q}) \setminus \{\bm0\}$ with $\bm{x}\in V_s - V_{s-1}$.
Since $s<n$, there exists
a vector $\bm{y}\in \mathbb{Q}^n \setminus \{\bm0\}$ with $H(\bm{x})\bm{y}=\bm0$.
Then $H(\bm{y})\bm{x} = H(\bm{x})\bm{y} = \bm0$, whence $\det H(\bm{y}) = 0$.
But $F(\bm{y})\ne 0$, since $X(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$.
Hence $L(\bm{y})=0$, so $\bm{y}\in M$.

Since $M$ is a linear space contained in $V_s$,
we have $M = T_{\bm{x}} M \subset T_{\bm{x}} V_s$.
Lemma~\ref{LEM:dav-bad-tangent-space},
with $(s,\bm{x},\bm{y},\bm{y},\bm{y})$ in place of $(r,\bm{x},\bm{v},\bm{y},\bm{z})$,
gives $0 = \bm{y}^t H(\bm{y}) \bm{y} = 6F(\bm{y})$.
This contradicts $F(\bm{y})\ne 0$.
It follows that $r(F) > (2n+1)/3$,
which implies Lemma~\ref{LEM:my-guy-slop}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- rem-4: body_md -->
As stated,
\cite[Proposition~4.3]{myguyzak}
is false for general integral domains $A$ and prime ideals $\mathfrak p$.
Its proof relies on the identity $v_{\mathfrak p}((\det M)^{n-1}) = (n-1)v_{\mathfrak p}(\det M)$, where $v_{\mathfrak p}(a) := \max\{k\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0} \cup \{\infty\}: a\in \mathfrak p^k\}$ for $a\in A$.
This is true if $\mathfrak p$ is principal, for instance,
but not in general.
<!-- end rem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{LEM:no-slop}
Assume that $X(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$.
Let $A\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$, and assign a real
weight $w_i$ to each variable $x_i$. The weight of a cubic monomial
$x_i x_j x_k$ is defined to be $w_i+w_j+w_k$. 
If every monomial occurring with a nonzero coefficient in
$F(A\bm{x})$ has nonnegative weight, then
\begin{equation}
\label{EQ:mean-weight}
w_1+\cdots+w_n\geqslant 0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
First suppose $A\in \operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{Q})$.
Then $A\bm{e}_i \in \mathbb{Q}^n \setminus \{\bm0\}$ for each standard basis vector $\bm{e}_i \in \mathbb{Q}^n$.
Thus $F(A\bm{e}_i) \ne 0$, since $X(\mathbb{Q}) = \emptyset$.
But $F(A\bm{e}_i)$ is precisely the coefficient of $x_i^3$ in $F(A\bm{x})$,
which has weight  $3w_i \geqslant 0$ for all $i$, by assumption. 
Summing over $i$ leads to \eqref{EQ:mean-weight}
in this case.
It remains to reduce the general case
to the case $A\in \operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{Q})$,
by a careful Galois descent procedure.

Let $I$ be a subset of
the set of all monomials $x_ix_jx_k$,
where $1\leqslant i,j,k\leqslant n$.
(After reordering $i,j,k$ we could assume $i\leqslant j\leqslant k$,
but that would cause confusion below.)
Let $W\in \mathbb{R}$.
Given $I$, let $S_I$ be the set of matrices $A\in \operatorname{GL}_n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$
for which every monomial appearing in $F(A\bm{x})$
lies in the set $I$.
Given $I$ and $W$, let $T_{I,W}$ be the set of vectors $\bm{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ for which the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every monomial $x_ix_jx_k\in I$
satisfies $v_i+v_j+v_k \geqslant 0$.
\item We have $\sum_{1\leqslant i\leqslant n} v_i = W$.
\end{enumerate}
Letting $I$ range over all possible subsets of monomials,
define the (not necessarily disjoint) union
$${\textstyle \mathcal{S}_W := \bigcup_I (S_I \times T_{I,W}).}$$
Every pair $(A,\bm{w})$ in the statement of Lemma~\ref{LEM:no-slop}
lies in $\mathcal{S}_W$
for some choice of $W$.
We then wish to show that $W\geqslant 0$.
Note however that in the definition of $S_I$,
the monomial support of $F(A\bm{x})$
is only required to be a subset of $I$,
not necessarily equal to $I$.

Two general symmetries will be useful.
First, if $(A,\bm{v})\in S_I \times T_{I,W}$,
then $$(AP,P^{-1}\bm{v})\in S_{I\circ P} \times T_{I\circ P,W}$$
for every permutation matrix $P$,
where $I\circ P := \{m\circ P: m\in I\}$.
Indeed, if the $(i,\pi(i))$ entry of $P$ is $1$,
where $\pi$ is a permutation,
then $(P\bm{x})_i = x_{\pi(i)}$ and $(P^{-1}\bm{v})_{\pi(i)} = v_i$,
and a monomial $m=x_ix_jx_k$ in $F(A\bm{x})$
is transformed to $m\circ P = x_{\pi(i)}x_{\pi(j)}x_{\pi(k)}$ in $F(AP\bm{x})$,
so that $$(P^{-1}\bm{v})_{\pi(i)} + (P^{-1}\bm{v})_{\pi(j)} + (P^{-1}\bm{v})_{\pi(k)}
= v_i + v_j + v_k \geqslant 0.$$
Second, let $\mathcal{B}(\bm{v})$ be the group of matrices $U = (u_{ij}) \in \operatorname{GL}_n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$
such that $u_{ij} \ne 0 \Rightarrow v_i \leqslant v_j$.
For example, if $v_1\leqslant v_2\leqslant \cdots \leqslant v_n$,
then any invertible upper triangular matrix lies in $\mathcal{B}(\bm{v})$,
and if $v_1<v_2<\cdots<v_n$ then every matrix in $\mathcal{B}(\bm{v})$ is upper triangular.
We claim that if $U \in \mathcal{B}(\bm{v})$
and $J$ denotes the monomial support of $F(AU\bm{x})$,
then $$(AU,\bm{v})\in S_J \times T_{J,W}.$$
Indeed, if $x_ix_jx_k \in I$,
then every monomial appearing
in the transformed polynomial $$(x_ix_jx_k) \circ U
= (U\bm{x})_i(U\bm{x})_j(U\bm{x})_k$$
may be written in the form $x_{i'}x_{j'}x_{k'}$,
where $v_i\leqslant v_{i'}$, $v_j\leqslant v_{j'}$ and $v_k\leqslant v_{k'}$,
by the definition of $\mathcal{B}(\bm{v})$.
It follows that $v_{i'} + v_{j'} + v_{k'}
\geqslant v_i + v_j + v_k \geqslant 0$, as desired.

With these two general symmetries established,
suppose now that $(A,\bm{v}),(A',\bm{v}')\in S_I \times T_{I,W}$.
Then there exist $U\in\mathcal{B}(\bm{v})$,
$U'\in\mathcal{B}(\bm{v}')$
and a permutation matrix $P$ such that
$AUP = A'U'$.
Indeed, first order the coordinates for $\bm{v}$ and $\bm{v}'$
separately so that their entries are non-decreasing.
In these orderings, both $\mathcal B(\bm{v})$ and
$\mathcal B(\bm{v}')$ contain the group of invertible upper
triangular matrices.
The usual {\em Bruhat decomposition} therefore gives
\[
A^{-1}A'=UPV,
\]
with $U\in\mathcal B(\bm{v})$, $V\in\mathcal B(\bm{v}')$
and $P$ a permutation matrix.
This remains a decomposition of the same form after undoing
the coordinate permutations.
Taking $U'=V^{-1}$ gives $AUP=A'U'$.

Let $A'' := AUP = A'U'$.
By the symmetries in the penultimate paragraph,
$(A'',P^{-1}\bm{v})=(AUP,P^{-1}\bm{v})\in \mathcal{S}_W$
and $(A'',\bm{v}')=(A'U',\bm{v}')\in \mathcal{S}_W$.
If $I''$ denotes the monomial support of $F(A''\bm{x})$,
then $$(A'',\tfrac12(P^{-1}\bm{v}+\bm{v}'))
\in S_{I''} \times T_{I'',W} \subset \mathcal{S}_W,$$
since $T_{I'',W}$ is convex.
Moreover, by the parallelogram law and the identity $\|P^{-1}\bm{v}\|_2 = \|\bm{v}\|_2$,
\begin{equation*}
\|\tfrac12(P^{-1}\bm{v}+\bm{v}')\|_2^2
= \tfrac12(\|P^{-1}\bm{v}\|_2^2 + \|\bm{v}'\|_2^2) - \|\tfrac12(P^{-1}\bm{v}-\bm{v}')\|_2^2
\leqslant \tfrac12(\|\bm{v}\|_2^2 + \|\bm{v}'\|_2^2),
\end{equation*}
with equality if and only if $P^{-1}\bm{v} = \bm{v}'$.

Each set $T_{I,W}$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$,
and thus if $T_{I,W} \ne \emptyset$ then
$T_{I,W}$ contains a vector of minimal Euclidean length.
Since there are only finitely many possible sets $I$, it follows that
there exists $(A,\bm{v})\in \mathcal{S}_W$ for which $\|\bm{v}\|_2$ is minimal.
Suppose $(A,\bm{v})\in S_I \times T_{I,W}$.
Then for any $\sigma\in \mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$,
we have $(\sigma(A),\bm{v}) \in S_I \times T_{I,W}$.
Taking $(\sigma(A),\bm{v})$ for $(A',\bm{v}')$ in the previous paragraph,
we get $P^{-1}\bm{v}=\bm{v}$,
since $\|\tfrac12(P^{-1}\bm{v}+\bm{v})\|_2 \geqslant \|\bm{v}\|_2$ by minimality of $\|\bm{v}\|_2$.

It follows from the definition of $\mathcal{B}(\bm{v})$ that, for every
$U\in\mathcal{B}(\bm{v})$ and every $r\in\mathbb{R}$,
\begin{equation}
U\text{span}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}\{e_j:v_j\leqslant r\}=\text{span}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}\{e_j:v_j\leqslant r\}.
\label{eq : pizzaefichi}
\end{equation}
Indeed, if $v_j\leqslant r$, then $Ue_j=\sum_i u_{i,j}e_i$. Since $U\in\mathcal{B}(\bm{v})$, we have $u_{i,j}\neq 0$ only if $v_i\leqslant v_j$. Hence
\[
Ue_j\in\text{span}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}\{e_i:v_i\leqslant v_j\}
\subseteq\operatorname{span}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}\{e_i:v_i\leqslant r\}.
\]
This proves the inclusion from left to right in \eqref{eq : pizzaefichi}.
The equality follows since $U^{-1}\in \mathcal{B}(\bm{v})\subset\operatorname{GL}_{n}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$.
Since $AUP=\sigma(A)U'$, with $U,U'\in\mathcal{B}(\bm{v})$, it follows from \eqref{eq : pizzaefichi} and the identity $P\bm{v}=\bm{v}$ that the filtration
\[
D_{\leqslant r}:=\operatorname{span}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}\{Ae_j:v_j\leqslant r\}\subseteq\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n
\]
is $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$-stable, where $r$ ranges over all real numbers.
 By Galois descent, there exists a filtration of $\mathbb{Q}$-vector spaces
$E_{\leqslant r} \subset \mathbb{Q}^n$
such that $E_{\leqslant r} \otimes \overline{\mathbb{Q}} = D_{\leqslant r}$.
Let $B\in \operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{Q})$ be a matrix whose columns $B\bm{e}_j$ split this filtration,
so that
$$\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{Q}}\{B\bm{e}_j: v_j\leqslant r\} = E_{\leqslant r}.$$
By the definition of $\mathcal{B}(\bm{v})$,
we may thus write $B = AM$ for some $M\in \mathcal{B}(\bm{v})$.
Therefore,
$$(B,\bm{v})=(AM,\bm{v}) \in \mathcal{S}_W,$$
by the symmetry properties observed earlier.
On replacing $A$ with $B$,
it follows that we may assume $A\in \operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{Q})$,
whence $W \geqslant 0$,
completing the proof of Lemma~\ref{LEM:no-slop}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- rem-5: body_md -->
\label{RMK:GIT-view}
The content of Lemma~\ref{LEM:no-slop} is best viewed through the lens of geometric invariant theory (GIT), as we shall now explain. Over $\mathbb{Q}$, the group $\operatorname{SL}_n$ acts on the space $W_n$ of cubic forms in $n$ variables via
$(g\cdot F)(\bm{x})=F(g^{-1}\bm{x})$. A form $F$ is called \emph{semistable} if the zero form does not belong to the Zariski closure of the
$\operatorname{SL}_n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$-orbit of $F$.  Lemma~\ref{LEM:no-slop} is then equivalent to saying that a cubic form without a nontrivial integer zero is semistable and an alternative proof of Lemma~\ref{LEM:no-slop} can be obtained using Kempf's rational version of the geometric Hilbert--Mumford criterion ~\cite[Corollary~4.3]{Kem78}. Indeed, the elementary proof above is essentially a simplified version of the proof of this result. See \cite[\S4]{BMRT} for related optimality and rationality results.

Intuitively, semistability prevents the cubic form from having very degenerate singularities and this is reflected in the next set of results, where we draw various conclusions about the geometry of the singular locus and the Hessian loci associated to our cubic form $F$. This connection between GIT stability and singularities has been used before, for example in Laza's work~\cite{Laz09} on the GIT compactification of the moduli space of cubic fourfolds. Additionally, a slightly weaker version of Lemma~\ref{LEM:no-slop-singular-linear} was obtained by Park~\cite[Lemma~7.2]{Par25}, also using semistability.
<!-- end rem-5 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{LEM:hessian-concentration}
There exist an integer $0\leqslant r\leqslant n$
and an irreducible or empty closed subset $Z \subset X$,
whose affine cone $\widehat Z$ lies in $V_r$ but not in $V_{r-1}$,
such that $\dim I = \dim \widehat Z + n-r$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Since $\{\bm0\}\times\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n\subset I$, we have $\dim I\geqslant n$.
If $\dim I=n$, then we may take $Z=\emptyset$ and $r=0$,
in the light of our convention $\widehat \emptyset=\{\bm0\}$.
Thus, we henceforth assume that $\dim I>n$.

Put $\bm{v}=\bm{y}+\bm{x}$ and $\bm{w}=\bm{y}-\bm{x}$.
The identities
$$
\nabla F(\bm{v})-\nabla F(\bm{w})=2H(\bm{y})\bm{x},
\qquad
F(\bm{v})-F(\bm{w})=2F(\bm{x})+\bm{y}^tH(\bm{y})\bm{x},
$$
together with $H(\bm{y})\bm{x}=H(\bm{x})\bm{y}$, identify $I$ with
$$
J:=\{(\bm{v},\bm{w})\in\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^{2n}:
\nabla F(\bm{v})=\nabla F(\bm{w})\},
$$
and $I\vert_{\widehat X\times\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n}$ with
$$
J_0:=\{(\bm{v},\bm{w})\in J:F(\bm{v})=F(\bm{w})\}.
$$
We claim that $\dim J_0=\dim J$.
For $\bm{z}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n$, put
$$
Y_{\bm{z}}:=\{\bm{x}\in\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n:\nabla F(\bm{x})=\bm{z}\}.
$$
On any irreducible component $C$ of $Y_{\bm{z}}$,
Euler's identity gives $3F=\bm{z}\cdot\bm{x}$.
Differentiating in the function field of $C$ gives
$$
3\mathrm{d} F=\bm{z}\cdot\mathrm{d}\bm{x}=\mathrm{d} F.
$$
Thus $\mathrm{d} F=0$, so $F$ is constant on $C$, since the ground
field is algebraically closed of characteristic zero.
Now project $J$ and $J_0$ to their common gradient.
For each nonempty $Y_{\bm{z}}$, choose a component $C$ of
dimension $d=\dim Y_{\bm{z}}$.
Then
$
C\times C\subset (J_0)_{\bm{z}}
\subset J_{\bm{z}}=Y_{\bm{z}}\times Y_{\bm{z}},
$
so both fibres have dimension $2d$.
The constructible sets
$$
S_d:=\{\bm{z}\in\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n:\dim Y_{\bm{z}}=d\},
\qquad 0\leqslant d\leqslant n,
$$
therefore give
$$
\dim J_0
=\max_{S_d\ne\emptyset}(\dim S_d+2d)
=\dim J.
$$
Consequently, $\dim I=\dim I\vert_{\widehat X\times\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n}$.
Stratifying the projective incidence correspondence on $X$ by rank,
and taking affine cones on a top-dimensional stratum,
completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{LEM:433-incidence-bound}
Assume $X(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$.
We have
\begin{align}
1 + \dim \operatorname{Sing} X \leqslant \max\{0, (2n-3)/3\},
\label{EQ:clean-slop-sing-bound} \\
\dim I\vert_{\operatorname{Sing}(\widehat X) \times \operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n} \leqslant \max\{n, (4n-6)/3\},
\label{EQ:clean-slop-sing-incidence-bound} \\
\dim I \leqslant \max\{n, (4n-3)/3\}.
\label{EQ:clean-slop-incidence-bound}
\end{align}
Moreover, fix an integer $0\leqslant r\leqslant n$
and an irreducible closed subset $Z \subset X$,
whose affine cone $\widehat Z$ lies in $V_r$ but not in $V_{r-1}$.
If $Z \subset \operatorname{Sing} X$, then
\begin{equation}
\label{EQ:slop-sing-bound}
\dim \widehat Z \leqslant \min\{n-r,2r-3\}.
\end{equation}
If $Z \not\subset \operatorname{Sing} X$, then
\begin{equation}
\label{EQ:slop-smooth-bound}
\dim \widehat Z \leqslant \min\{r+(n-3)/3,2r-2\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The bound \eqref{EQ:clean-slop-sing-bound} is trivial if $\operatorname{Sing} X = \emptyset$,
and otherwise it follows from \eqref{EQ:slop-sing-bound},
since $$\min\{n-r,2r-3\}
\leqslant \tfrac23(n-r) + \tfrac13(2r-3) = \tfrac13(2n-3).$$
The bound \eqref{EQ:clean-slop-sing-incidence-bound} is trivial if $\dim I \leqslant n$,
and otherwise it follows from \eqref{EQ:slop-sing-bound},
since $$\min\{n-r,2r-3\} + n-r \leqslant \tfrac13(n-r) + \tfrac23(2r-3) + n-r
= \tfrac13(4n-6).$$
The bound \eqref{EQ:clean-slop-incidence-bound} is trivial if $\dim I \leqslant n$,
and otherwise it follows from Lemma~\ref{LEM:hessian-concentration},
together with \eqref{EQ:clean-slop-sing-incidence-bound}
and the first bound in \eqref{EQ:slop-smooth-bound},
since $r+(n-3)/3 + n-r = (4n-3)/3$.

It remains to prove \eqref{EQ:slop-sing-bound} and \eqref{EQ:slop-smooth-bound}.
Write $\Phi(\bm{y},\bm{v},\bm{z}) := \bm{y}^tH(\bm{v})\bm{z}$
for the symmetric trilinear form associated to $F$.
Choose a nonzero smooth point $\bm{x}$ of $\widehat Z$ with $\operatorname{rank} H(\bm{x})=r$,
and with $\nabla F(\bm{x})\ne \bm0$ if $Z\not\subset\operatorname{Sing} X$.
Set
\begin{equation*}
T:=T_{\bm{x}}(\widehat Z),
\qquad L:=\ker H(\bm{x}).
\end{equation*}
Lemma~\ref{LEM:dav-bad-tangent-space} gives $\Phi(L,T,L)=0$.
Also, $\Phi(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n,\bm{x},L)=0$, because $H(\bm{x})L=\bm0$.
Finally, since $F\vert_{\widehat Z}=0$, we have $F(\bm{x}+\varepsilon\bm{v}) \equiv 0\bmod{\varepsilon^2}$
for all $\bm{v}\in T$, so $\bm{v}^t \nabla F(\bm{x}) = 0$.
Thus $\Phi(T,\bm{x},\bm{x})=0$,
in view of the identity $H(\bm{x})\bm{x}=2\nabla F(\bm{x})$.

Before proceeding, we collect some basic facts about $T$ and $L$.
Since $\widehat Z$ is cut out by homogeneous equations,
Euler's identity gives $\bm{x}\in T$.
By smoothness of $\widehat Z$ at $\bm{x}$, we have $\dim T = \dim \widehat Z$.
Since $\operatorname{rank} H(\bm{x})=r$, we have $\dim L = n-r$.

Suppose first that $Z\subset\operatorname{Sing} X$.
Then $\nabla F(\bm{x}+\varepsilon\bm{v}) \equiv 0\bmod{\varepsilon^2}$
for all $\bm{v}\in T$,
so $H(\bm{x})\bm{v} = \bm0$.
Thus $T\subset L$, so $\dim \widehat Z\leqslant n-r$.
It remains to prove that $\dim \widehat Z \leqslant 2r-3$.
Split the flag $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\bm{x} \subset T \subset L \subset \overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n$,
writing
\[
W_{-4} := \overline{\mathbb{Q}}\bm{x},\qquad
T=W_{-4}\oplus W_{-1},\qquad
L=T\oplus W_0,\qquad
\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n=L\oplus W_2,
\]
so that $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n = W_{-4} \oplus W_{-1} \oplus W_0 \oplus W_2$.
Let $A\in \operatorname{GL}_n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ be a matrix such that
$$\{A\bm{e}_1,\dots,A\bm{e}_n\}
\subset W_{-4} \cup W_{-1} \cup W_0 \cup W_2.$$
Let $w_i := \nu$ if $A\bm{e}_i\in W_\nu$, where $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$ and $\nu\in \{-4,-1,0,2\}$.
Let $1\leqslant i,j,k\leqslant n$ with $w_i\leqslant w_j\leqslant w_k$
and suppose $\Phi(A\bm{e}_i,A\bm{e}_j,A\bm{e}_k) \ne 0$.
If $w_i=-4$,
then $w_j=w_k=2$, since $\Phi(\bm{x},L,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n)=0$ and $L = W_{-4} \oplus W_{-1} \oplus W_0$.
Thus $w_i+w_j+w_k = -4+2+2 = 0$ in this case.
If $w_i=-1$, then $w_k=2$, since $\Phi(T,L,L)=0$.
Thus $w_i+w_j+w_k \geqslant -1-1+2 = 0$ in this case.
If $w_i\geqslant 0$, then $w_i+w_j+w_k\geqslant 0$ trivially.
Lemma~\ref{LEM:no-slop} therefore gives
\[
-4-\dim W_{-1}+2\dim W_2 \geqslant 0.
\]
Since $\dim W_{-1} = \dim \widehat Z - 1$ and $\dim W_2 = r$,
we get $\dim \widehat Z \leqslant 2r-3$.

Suppose now that $Z\not\subset\operatorname{Sing} X$.
Since $H(\bm{x})\bm{x}=2\nabla F(\bm{x})\ne \bm0$, we have $\bm{x}\notin L$.
Split the flag $(T\cap L)\oplus\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\bm{x} \subset T \subset T+L \subset \overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n$,
writing
\[
W_{-2} := (T\cap L)\oplus\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\bm{x},\qquad
T = W_{-2}\oplus W_1,\qquad
L = (T\cap L)\oplus W_0,\qquad
\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n = (T+L) \oplus W_4,
\]
so that $T+L = T\oplus W_0$.
By trilinearity of $\Phi$,
we have $\Phi(W_{-2},L+\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\bm{x},T+L)=0$ since
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\Phi(T\cap L,L,T) \subset \Phi(L,L,T)=0$,
\item $\Phi(T\cap L,L,L) \subset \Phi(T,L,L)=0$,
\item $\Phi(T\cap L,\bm{x},T+L) \subset \Phi(L,\bm{x},\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n)=0$,
\item $\Phi(\bm{x},L,T+L) \subset \Phi(\bm{x},L,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n)=0$,
\item $\Phi(\bm{x},\bm{x},T)=0$, and
\item $\Phi(\bm{x},\bm{x},L) \subset \Phi(\bm{x},\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n,L)=0$.
\end{enumerate}
Since $L+\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\bm{x}=W_{-2} \oplus W_0$ and $T+L=W_{-2} \oplus W_0 \oplus W_1$,
it follows that
\begin{equation}
\label{EQ:clever-slop}
\Phi(W_{-2},W_{-2} \oplus W_0,W_{-2} \oplus W_0 \oplus W_1)=0.
\end{equation}
Let $A\in \operatorname{GL}_n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ be a matrix such that
$$\{A\bm{e}_1,\dots,A\bm{e}_n\}
\subset W_{-2} \cup W_0 \cup W_1 \cup W_4.$$
Let $w_i := \nu$ if $A\bm{e}_i\in W_\nu$, where $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$ and $\nu\in \{-2,0,1,4\}$.
Let $1\leqslant i,j,k\leqslant n$ with $w_i\leqslant w_j\leqslant w_k$
and suppose $\Phi(A\bm{e}_i,A\bm{e}_j,A\bm{e}_k) \ne 0$.
If $w_i=-2$ and $w_j\leqslant 0$, then $w_k=4$ by \eqref{EQ:clever-slop}.
Thus $w_i+w_j+w_k \geqslant -2-2+4 = 0$ in this case.
If $w_i=-2$ and $w_j\geqslant 1$, then $w_i+w_j+w_k \geqslant -2+1+1 = 0$.
If $w_i\geqslant 0$, then $w_i+w_j+w_k\geqslant 0$ trivially.
Lemma~\ref{LEM:no-slop} therefore gives
\begin{equation*}
-2\dim W_{-2} + \dim W_1 + 4 \dim W_4 \geqslant 0.
\end{equation*}
Let $a := \dim(T\cap L)$ and $t := \dim T = \dim \widehat Z$.
Then $\dim W_{-2} = a + 1$,
$\dim W_1 = t - a - 1$
and $\dim W_4 = n - \dim (T+L) = n - t - \dim L + a
= r - t + a$.
Thus
\begin{equation*}
0\leqslant -2(a+1) + (t-a-1) + 4(r-t+a)
= -3+a-3t+4r.
\end{equation*}
Since $\bm{x}\in T$ but $\bm{x}\notin L$, we have $a\leqslant t-1$,
so $0 \leqslant -4-2t+4r$ and $t\leqslant 2r-2$.
On the other hand, $a\leqslant \dim L = n-r$,
so $0 \leqslant -3+n-3t+3r$ and $t\leqslant r + (n-3)/3$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:hesrank}
Assume that $n\geqslant 3$
and $X(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$.
Let $1\leqslant r \leqslant n-1$.
Then
$$\dim V_r\leqslant \min \left\{\left\lfloor \frac{n}{3}\right\rfloor +r-1, n-1\right\}$$
and $V_0 = V_1\cap \widehat X = \{\bm0\}$.
Moreover, $\dim(V_r\cap \widehat X)\leqslant \min\{2r-2,n-2\}$ if $r<2\lceil n/3\rceil$.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Since $F$ is good (see Definition~\ref{defn : good}),
the polynomial $\det(H(\bm{x}))$ does not vanish identically.
In particular, if $\bm{x}\in V_r$, then $\det(H(\bm{x}))=0$ must hold and hence $\dim V_r\leqslant n-1$.
Furthermore, $V_0$ is a linear space defined over $\mathbb{Q}$,
so $V_0 = \{\bm0\}$ by the $r=0$ case of Definition~\ref{defn : good}.

Next consider the projection $\pi\colon I\to \operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n$ defined by $(\bm{x},\bm{y})\mapsto \bm{x}$. Then clearly 
$$V_r=
\{\bm{x}\in \operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n\colon \dim \pi^{-1}(\bm{x})\geqslant n-r\}.
$$
Thus $\dim V_r \leqslant \dim I - (n-r)\leqslant \lfloor n/3 \rfloor +r-1$
by \eqref{Eq: Def.hessian.Incidence} and \eqref{EQ:clean-slop-incidence-bound},
since $n \leqslant (4n-3)/3$.

The claims $\dim(V_r\cap \widehat X) \leqslant 2r-2$
and $V_1\cap \widehat X = \{\bm0\}$
follow from \eqref{EQ:slop-sing-bound} and \eqref{EQ:slop-smooth-bound}.
The final claim follows directly from
Lemma~\ref{LEM:my-guy-slop}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{LEM:no-slop-singular-linear}
Assume $X(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$.
If $\nabla F$ vanishes on
a $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-vector space $L\subset\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n$,
then $$\dim L\leqslant n/3.$$
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $\Phi$ be as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{LEM:433-incidence-bound}.
Then $\Phi(L,L,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n) = 0$,
since $$2H(\bm{x})\bm{y} = \nabla F(\bm{x}+\bm{y}) - \nabla F(\bm{x}-\bm{y}) = \bm0-\bm0 = \bm0$$
for all $\bm{x},\bm{y}\in L$.
Write $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n=L\oplus M$.
Choose $A\in \operatorname{GL}_n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ with
$\{A\bm{e}_1,\dots,A\bm{e}_n\}
\subset L \cup M$.
Let $w_i := -2$ if $A\bm{e}_i\in L$, and $w_i := 1$ if $A\bm{e}_i\in M$.
Let $1\leqslant i,j,k\leqslant n$ with $w_i\leqslant w_j\leqslant w_k$
and suppose $\Phi(A\bm{e}_i,A\bm{e}_j,A\bm{e}_k) \ne 0$.
If $w_i = -2$, then $w_j=w_k=1$, since $\Phi(L,L,\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n) = 0$.
Thus $w_i+w_j+w_k=0$ in this case.
If $w_i=1$, then $w_i+w_j+w_k=3$.
Lemma~\ref{LEM:no-slop} therefore gives
$-2\dim L + \dim M \geqslant 0$.
Since $\dim M = n - \dim L$, it follows that $3\dim L \leqslant n$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{PROP:rational-exceptional-hyperplanes-general}
Suppose $t\geqslant\max\{0,\dim\operatorname{Sing} X\}$,
and let $A_t$ be the Zariski closure of $B_t(\mathbb{Q})$ in $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$.
Then $A_t$ is defined over $\mathbb{Q}$.
Moreover, $A_t(\mathbb{Q})=B_t(\mathbb{Q})$ and
\begin{equation}
\label{EQ:rational-terminal-bound}
1+\dim A_t\leqslant
\max\left\{0,n-\left\lceil\frac{3(t+2)}2\right\rceil\right\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The set $A_t$ is contained in the intersection of its Galois conjugates.
Thus $A_t$ is Galois-stable, and hence defined over $\mathbb{Q}$.
Moreover, $A_t \subset B_t$, since $B_t$ is closed.
Thus $A_t(\mathbb{Q}) \subset B_t(\mathbb{Q})$.
Since $B_t(\mathbb{Q}) \subset A_t(\mathbb{Q})$ by definition,
it follows that $A_t(\mathbb{Q})=B_t(\mathbb{Q})$.
It remains to prove \eqref{EQ:rational-terminal-bound}.

The set $A_t(\mathbb{Q})=B_t(\mathbb{Q})$
is Zariski dense in $A_t$.
Thus every nonempty open subset of $A_t$
contains a $\mathbb{Q}$-point.
This, together with \eqref{EQ:clean-slop-sing-bound},
will be the main arithmetic input used below.

Let $Z$ be an irreducible component of $(A_t)_{\rm sm}$.
As in \S\ref{sec : geom_cubic_hyper}, we work geometrically over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.
Let $\pi\colon S \to \operatorname{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$ be the projection $([\bm{x}],[\bm{v}]) \mapsto [\bm{v}]$.
For each $\bm{v}\in Z$, we have $\dim \pi^{-1}(\bm{v}) = \dim \operatorname{Sing}(X\cap H_{\bm{v}}) \geqslant t \geqslant 0$.
Since $Z$ is irreducible,
generic smoothness of the map $\pi\vert_{\pi^{-1}(Z)}$,
for the reduced scheme structures on $Z$ and $\pi^{-1}(Z)$,
produces an irreducible open subset $U$ of $\pi^{-1}(Z)$
for which $\pi\vert_U$ is smooth of relative dimension $\geqslant t$
and the image $Z'$ of $\pi\vert_U$ is a dense open subset of $Z$.
In particular, $\pi\vert_U$ is flat,
with some constant fibre dimension $e\geqslant t$.

Let $\widehat Z'$ denote the affine cone of $Z'$.
Let $\bm{v}\in \widehat Z' \setminus \{\bm0\}$
and $M_{\bm{v}} := (T_{\bm{v}} \widehat Z')^\perp \subset \operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n$.
We claim that
\begin{equation}
\label{EQ:rational-contact-restriction}
\dim\{\bm{x}\in M_{\bm{v}}:\nabla F(\bm{x})\in M_{\bm{v}}^\perp\}\geqslant e+1.
\end{equation}
For a linear subspace $L\subset \overline{\mathbb{Q}}^n$,
we have $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} F(\bm{x}+t\bm{v}) \vert_{t=0}
= \bm{v}\cdot \nabla F(\bm{x})$ for all $\bm{x},\bm{v}\in L$.
If $F\vert_L\ne 0$,
then $F\vert_L$ is singular at $\bm{x}$
if and only if $\nabla F(\bm{x})$ is orthogonal to $L$.
Thus if $F\vert_{M_{\bm{v}}} \ne 0$,
then the left-hand side of \eqref{EQ:rational-contact-restriction}
equals $\dim\operatorname{Sing}\{\bm{x}\in M_{\bm{v}}:F(\bm{x})=0\}$.

Suppose first that $U$ is not contained in
$\operatorname{Sing}(X) \times Z'$.
Then by shrinking $U$ and $Z'$ if necessary, we may assume that
$U \subset X_{\rm sm} \times Z'$.
For $([\bm{x}],[\bm{v}])\in U$, each $\bm{w}\in T_{\bm{v}} \widehat Z'$
lifts via $\pi\vert_U$ to a tangent vector $(\bm{y},\bm{w})$
of (the bi-affine cone of $U$ in) $\widehat X_{\rm sm} \times \widehat Z'$
at $(\bm{x},\bm{v})$,
since $\pi\vert_U$ is smooth.
By the definition of $S$,
we have $F(\bm{x}) = \bm{x}\cdot\bm{v} = 0$,
and $\nabla F(\bm{x})=\alpha\bm{v}$ for some $\alpha\ne 0$.
Differentiating the first two equations in the direction $(\bm{y},\bm{w})$,
using the chain and product rules, gives
\begin{equation*}
0 = \bm{y} \cdot \nabla F(\bm{x})
= \alpha \bm{y} \cdot \bm{v}
= - \alpha \bm{x} \cdot \bm{w}.
\end{equation*}
Thus $\bm{x}\in (T_{\bm{v}} \widehat Z')^\perp = M_{\bm{v}}$.
On the other hand, $\nabla F(\bm{x}) = \alpha\bm{v} \in T_{\bm{v}} \widehat Z'$,
since $\bm{v}\in \widehat Z'$ and $\widehat Z'$ is a cone.
Thus $\nabla F(\bm{x})$ is orthogonal to $M_{\bm{v}}$.
The affine cone of the fibre $\pi\vert_U^{-1}(\bm{v})$
therefore lies in the locus in \eqref{EQ:rational-contact-restriction},
proving that inequality.

Now suppose $U\subset\operatorname{Sing}(X)\times Z'$.
Then $\dim U \leqslant \dim \operatorname{Sing} X + \dim Z'$.
On the other hand, $\dim U = e + \dim Z'
\geqslant t + \dim Z'
\geqslant \dim \operatorname{Sing} X + \dim Z'$,
since $e \geqslant t$
and $t \geqslant \dim \operatorname{Sing} X$.
Thus equality holds.
The closure of $U$ in $\operatorname{Sing}(X)\times Z'$
therefore contains some irreducible component $X' \times Z'$
of $\operatorname{Sing}(X)\times Z'$, with $\dim X' = \dim \operatorname{Sing} X$.
Since $\bm{x} \cdot \bm{v}$ vanishes on $U$,
it vanishes on $X' \times Z'$ by continuity.
Differentiating the equation $\bm{x} \cdot \bm{v} = 0$
with respect to $\bm{v}\in \widehat Z' \setminus \{\bm0\}$, keeping $\bm{x}\in \widehat X'$ fixed,
shows that $\widehat X' \subset (T_{\bm{v}} \widehat Z')^\perp = M_{\bm{v}}$.
On the other hand, the definition of $\operatorname{Sing} X$
implies that $\nabla F(\bm{x}) = \bm0$ vanishes for all $\bm{x}\in \widehat X'$,
so that $\nabla F(\bm{x})$ is trivially orthogonal to $M_{\bm{v}}$.
It follows that $\widehat X'$
lies in the locus in \eqref{EQ:rational-contact-restriction},
proving that inequality.

Since $Z'$ is open in $A_t$, we may choose $\bm{v}$ to be a $\mathbb{Q}$-point.
The vector space $M_{\bm{v}}$ is then defined over $\mathbb{Q}$.
The inequality \eqref{EQ:rational-contact-restriction}
trivially implies $\dim M_{\bm{v}} \geqslant 1$, since $e\geqslant t\geqslant 0$.
Moreover, $F\vert_{M_{\bm{v}}} \ne 0$, since $X(\mathbb{Q}) = \emptyset$.
Thus \eqref{EQ:rational-contact-restriction} in fact implies
$\dim M_{\bm{v}} - 1
\geqslant \dim\operatorname{Sing}\{\bm{x}\in M_{\bm{v}}:F(\bm{x})=0\}
\geqslant e+1$, whence $\dim M_{\bm{v}} \geqslant 2$.
Plugging the inequality \eqref{EQ:clean-slop-sing-bound} for $F\vert_{M_{\bm{v}}} \ne 0$
into \eqref{EQ:rational-contact-restriction} now gives
\begin{equation*}
\frac{2(n-1-\dim Z) - 3}{3}
= \frac{2\dim M_{\bm{v}} - 3}{3}
\geqslant e+1 \geqslant t+1,
\end{equation*}
whence $2(1+\dim Z) \leqslant 2n-3(t+2)$.
This proves \eqref{EQ:rational-terminal-bound},
after taking into account the fact that $A_t$ could be empty,
in which case $1+\dim A_t = 0$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:2n/3}
We have $\dim X^*\geqslant 2\lceil n/3\rceil-2$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Thanks to a result of Segre \cite{SegreII}, we know that $\dim X^*=r(F)-2$. The claim now follows from Lemma~\ref{LEM:my-guy-slop}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{PROP:geometric-exceptional-hyperplanes-general}
If $t\geqslant (n+1)/3$, then
\begin{equation}
1+\dim W_t\leqslant\max\{0,n-t-2\}.
\label{EQ:geometric-gauss-bound}
\end{equation}
If $t\geqslant \max\{(n+1)/3,\dim\operatorname{Sing} X\}$, then
\begin{equation}
1+\dim B_t\leqslant\max\{0,n-t-2\}.
\label{EQ:geometric-terminal-bound}
\end{equation}
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Suppose first that $t\geqslant (n+1)/3$.
Since $X_{\rm sm}$ is irreducible,
the closure $\Gamma$ is irreducible,
with $\dim \Gamma = \dim X_{\rm sm} = n-2$.
Yet $\dim X^* \geqslant 2n/3-2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:2n/3}.
Consequently the general fibre of $\pi_2\colon \Gamma\to X^*$ has dimension
at most $n/3<t$.
The set $\pi_2^{-1}(W_t)$ is therefore a proper closed
subset of $\Gamma$, of dimension at most $\dim \Gamma - 1 = n-3$.
If $W_t$ is nonempty, every fibre over it has dimension
at least $t$, so
\[
\dim W_t+t
\leqslant \dim \pi_2^{-1}(W_t)
\leqslant n-3.
\]
This proves \eqref{EQ:geometric-gauss-bound},
since if $W_t = \emptyset$ then $1 + \dim W_t = 0$.

Now assume $t\geqslant \max\{(n+1)/3,\dim\operatorname{Sing} X\}$, and take $[\bm{v}]\in B_t$.
Choose an irreducible component $Z$ of $\operatorname{Sing}(X\cap H_{\bm{v}})$
with $\dim Z\geqslant t$.
If $Z$ meets $X_{\rm sm}$, then its dense open subset $Z\cap X_{\rm sm}$ lies in
$\Gamma_{[\bm{v}]}$, so $[\bm{v}]\in W_t$.
Now suppose $Z \subset \operatorname{Sing} X$.
Then $\dim\operatorname{Sing} X \geqslant \dim Z \geqslant t$,
where equality must hold in view of the assumption $t \geqslant \dim\operatorname{Sing} X$.
Thus $Z$ is one of the
finitely many $t$-dimensional components of $\operatorname{Sing} X$.
Its cone $\widehat Z$ cannot be linear: Lemma~\ref{LEM:no-slop-singular-linear}
would give $t+1 = \dim \widehat Z \leqslant n/3$, contrary to $t>n/3$.
Thus the linear span $L$ of $\widehat Z$ has dimension at least $t+2$.
Since $Z \subset H_{\bm{v}}$ by definition,
this constrains $\bm{v}$ to lie in the orthogonal complement $L^\perp$,
where $\dim L^\perp \leqslant n-\dim L \leqslant n-t-2$.
Taking the finite union over all possible
irreducible components $Z \subset \operatorname{Sing} X$
proves \eqref{EQ:geometric-terminal-bound}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{COR:general-n-exceptional-hyperplanes}
Assume $n\geqslant10$ and $X(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$.
Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:n10-sing-X}
\dim\operatorname{Sing}(X)\leqslant \lfloor(2n-6)/3\rfloor \leqslant n-6.
\end{equation}
The set $B_{n-6}(\mathbb{Q})$ is finite if $n=10$,
and is empty if $n\geqslant11$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-terminal-hyperplanes}
B_{n-5}(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset.
\end{equation}
Geometrically, we have $B_{n-4} = \emptyset$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:terminal-hyperplane-dimensions}
1+\dim B_{n-6}\leqslant4,
\qquad
1+\dim B_{n-5}\leqslant3.
\end{equation}
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The inequality \eqref{eq:n10-sing-X} follows from \eqref{EQ:clean-slop-sing-bound},
Indeed, for $n\geqslant 12$ we have $(2n-6)/3 \leqslant n-6$,
and for $n=10,11$ we have $\lfloor(2n-6)/3\rfloor = n-6$.
Since $n-6\geqslant(n+1)/3$,
taking $t=n-6,n-5$ in \eqref{EQ:geometric-terminal-bound} proves
\eqref{eq:terminal-hyperplane-dimensions}.
On the other hand,
the claim $B_{n-4} = \emptyset$ follows from \eqref{EQ:clean-slop-sing-bound}
and Theorem~\ref{Thm: ZaksBoundSingLocus}.
Separately,
Proposition~\ref{PROP:rational-exceptional-hyperplanes-general}
with $t=n-6,n-5$ gives
\[
1+\dim A_{n-6}
\leqslant \max\left\{0,\left\lfloor\frac{12-n}{2}\right\rfloor\right\},
\qquad
1+\dim A_{n-5}
\leqslant \max\left\{0,\left\lfloor\frac{9-n}{2}\right\rfloor\right\}.
\]
This proves the assertions about $\mathbb{Q}$-points.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:prime-modulus-pointwise}
We have the following estimates:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $p\mid\bm{v}$ then
$        S_p(\bm{v})=S_p(\bm 0)\ll p^{n-3/2}$.

\item If $p\nmid\bm{v}$ and $n\geqslant 10$, then
$
S_p(\bm{v})\ll p^{n-2}.
$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:geometry-all-hyperplane-sections}
There is a finite set of primes, depending only on $F$, such that for every
prime outside this set and every $\overline{\bm{v}}\neq\bm 0$, the cubic hypersurface
$Y_{\bm{v}}$
is geometrically integral.  Furthermore, if $Y_{\bm{v}}$ is a cone over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ with maximal vertex of 
projective dimension $s$, then
\begin{equation}
s\leqslant 1.
\label{eq:prime-sum-vertex-bound}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
After excluding finitely many primes,
spreading out \eqref{eq:n10-sing-X} gives
\begin{equation}
\dim\operatorname{Sing}(X_{p}) = \dim\operatorname{Sing}(X) \leqslant n-6.
\label{eq:prime-sum-sing-Xp}
\end{equation}
Likewise, if $V_{2,p}=\{\bm{x}\in\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p}: \operatorname{rank} H(\bm{x})\leqslant2\}$,
then spreading out Corollary~\ref{cor:hesrank} gives
\begin{equation}
\dim (V_{2,p} \cap \{F=0\}) = \dim (V_2 \cap \{F=0\}) \leqslant 2\cdot 2-2 = 2.
\label{eq:prime-sum-V2p}
\end{equation}
We may also suppose that $p>3$ and that $X_p$ is geometrically integral
of dimension $n-2$
and is not a cone,
by Proposition~\ref{Bro-integral-cone}.
Indeed, it is well known that geometric integrality
and dimension spread out,
whereas the set of vertices of $X$ spreads out by Remark~\ref{field-of-maximal-vertex}.

The hyperplane section $Y_{\bm{v}}$ is geometrically integral
by Theorem~\ref{Thm: ZaksBoundSingLocus},
because \eqref{eq:prime-sum-sing-Xp} gives
$$\dim X_p - \dim \operatorname{Sing}(X_p)
\geqslant (n-2) - (n-6) = 4.$$
Suppose now that $Y_{\bm{v}}$ is a cone over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$
with maximal vertex $\operatorname{\mathbb{P}}^s$.  Over
$\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$, choose coordinates $(\bm{u},\bm{z},t)$ such that $t=0$ cuts
out $\overline{\bm{v}}\cdot \bm{x}=0$, the variables $\bm{u}=(u_0,\ldots,u_s)$ run along the
vertex, and the minimal base is defined by a cubic form $C(\bm{z})$.  Then
\[
    F(\bm{u},\bm{z},t)=C(\bm{z})+tQ(\bm{u},\bm{z},t)
\]
for a quadratic form $Q$.  At every point $(\bm{u},\bm 0,0)$ of the affine cone
over the vertex, all entries of the Hessian matrix $H(\bm{u},\bm 0,0)$ vanish except possibly
those in the $t$-row and the $t$-column.  Thus $\operatorname{rank} H(\bm{u},\bm 0,0)\leqslant2$ and so the 
affine $(s+1)$-plane over the vertex is contained in $V_{2,p}$.
Since the vertex is trivially also contained in $\{F=0\}$,
it follows from  \eqref{eq:prime-sum-V2p} that 
\[
s+1\leqslant 2,
\]
which completes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
It is clearly enough to work outside a finite set of primes depending on $F$.  
To begin with it follows from 
Lemma \ref{lem:Fq} that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fvf}
\left|    \#X_p(\mathbb{F}_p)-\pi_{n-2}(p)\right|
       \ll_n p^{(n-1+\sigma_p)/2}\leqslant p^{n-7/2},
\end{equation}
since $\sigma_p=\dim\operatorname{Sing}(X_{p})\leqslant n-6$, 
by \eqref{eq:prime-sum-sing-Xp}.
Inserting this into  \eqref{eq:Sp-projective-v-zero} gives part (i).

Assume now that $\overline{\bm{v}}\neq\bm 0$.  By 
\eqref{eq:Sp-projective-v-nonzero} and \eqref{eq:fvf}, we have
\begin{equation}
    S_p(\bm{v})
      =p^2\bigl(\#Y_{\bm{v}}(\mathbb{F}_p)-\pi_{n-3}(p)\bigr)
       +O(p^{n-5/2}).
    \label{eq:prime-sum-reduced-to-Y}
\end{equation}
It remains to count points on $Y_{\bm{v}}$.
If $Y_{\bm{v}}$ is not a cone, the second estimate in
Lemma~\ref{lem:Fq} yields
\[
\left|    \#Y_{\bm{v}}(\mathbb{F}_p)-\pi_{n-3}(p)\right|\ll_n p^{n-4}.
\]
Suppose now that $Y_{\bm{v}}$ is a cone.
Its defining cubic form over $\mathbb{F}_p$
is absolutely irreducible by Lemma~\ref{lem:geometry-all-hyperplane-sections}.
Its maximal vertex is an $s$-plane defined over $\mathbb{F}_p$, where $s\geqslant 0$.
After choosing an $\mathbb{F}_p$-linear complement its minimal base is a geometrically
integral, non-conical cubic hypersurface
$Z_{\bm{v}}\subset\operatorname{\mathbb{P}}^{n-s-3}_{\mathbb{F}_p}$,
defined by a cubic form in $n-s-2$ variables.
Let
$$
b=n-s-4.
$$
Projection away from the maximal vertex shows that
\[
    \#Y_{\bm{v}}(\mathbb{F}_p)
       =\pi_s(p)+p^{s+1}\#Z_{\bm{v}}(\mathbb{F}_p),
\]
and $\pi_{n-3}(p)=\pi_s(p)+p^{s+1}\pi_b(p)$.
If $b\geqslant2$, then Lemma~\ref{lem:Fq} gives
\[
   \left| \#Z_{\bm{v}}(\mathbb{F}_p)-\pi_b(p)\right|\ll_n p^{b-1},
\]
from which it follows that 
\begin{equation}
\left|    \#Y_{\bm{v}}(\mathbb{F}_p)-\pi_{n-3}(p)\right|
      \ll_n p^{s+1+b-1}=p^{n-4}.
    \label{eq:prime-sum-Y-good}
\end{equation}
Yet by \eqref{eq:prime-sum-vertex-bound} and Remark~\ref{field-of-maximal-vertex},
we have $s\leqslant 1$
and $b=n-s-4\geqslant 2$ (in fact $b\geqslant 5$)
whenever $n\geqslant 10$.
Combining \eqref{eq:prime-sum-Y-good} with
\eqref{eq:prime-sum-reduced-to-Y} therefore proves part~(ii), uniformly for every
$\overline{\bm{v}}\neq\bm 0$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:prime-square-stratification}
Let $p$ be any prime and let $t\geqslant 0$.
If $p\nmid\bm{v}$ and $[\overline{\bm{v}}]\notin \mathcal W_{t,p}(\mathbb{F}_p)$,
then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:p2-strat-bound}
S_{p^2}(\bm{v})\ll_F p^{n+t+1}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every prime $p$ and every $\bm{v}\in\mathbb{Z}^n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:p2-cutoff}
S_{p^2}(\bm{v})\ll_F p^{2n-3}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
It is enough to prove the estimates outside a fixed finite set of primes.
We may therefore assume that
$p>3$, that $X_p$ is geometrically integral, and that $\dim\operatorname{Sing}(X_p)\leqslant n-6$.

Writing $a=b+pc$ and $\bm{x}=\bm{y}+p\bm{z}$,
and then summing over $c\in\mathbb{F}_p$ and $\bm{z}\in\mathbb{F}_p^n$, gives
\[
S_{p^2}(\bm{v})
= \sum_{a\in (\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z})^\ast}
\sum_{\bm{x}\in (\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z})^n}e_{p^2}\left(aF(\bm{x})+ \bm{v}\cdot \bm{x}\right)
= p^{n+1}
\sum_{b\in\mathbb{F}_p^\ast}
\sum_{\substack{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{F}_p^n\\
F(\bm{y})=0\\
b\nabla F(\bm{y})=-\overline{\bm{v}}}}
e_{p^2}\bigl(bF(\bm{y})+\bm{v}\cdot\bm{y}\bigr),
\]
since $aF(\bm{x})+ \bm{v}\cdot \bm{x}$ may be rewritten as
$$(b+pc)F(\bm{y}+p\bm{z}) + \bm{v}\cdot (\bm{y}+p\bm{z})
\equiv  bF(\bm{y}) + \bm{v}\cdot \bm{y}
+ p\left(b\nabla F(\bm{y})\cdot \bm{z}
+ cF(\bm{y}) + \bm{v}\cdot \bm{z}\right)  \bmod{p^2}.$$
The final sum over $b$ and $\bm{y}$ is well-defined:
in view of the conditions $F(\bm{y})=0$ and $b\nabla F(\bm{y})=-\overline{\bm{v}}$,
each summand $e_{p^2}\bigl(bF(\bm{y})+\bm{v}\cdot\bm{y}\bigr)$ 
only depends on $b,\bm{y}\bmod{p}$ and $\bm{v}\bmod{p^2}$.

By the triangle inequality and the Lang--Weil estimate,
\begin{equation*}
|S_{p^2}(\bm{v})|
\leqslant p^{n+1}
\sum_{b\in\mathbb{F}_p^\ast}
\sum_{\substack{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{F}_p^n\\
F(\bm{y})=0\\
b\nabla F(\bm{y})=-\overline{\bm{v}}}} 1
= p^{n+1}
(p-1)\,
\#V(\mathbb{F}_p)
\ll_n p^{n+2+\dim V},
\end{equation*}
where $V = \operatorname{Sing}(X_{p,\rm sm} \cap \{\overline{\bm{v}}\cdot\bm{x}=0\})$ if $p\nmid \bm{v}$,
and $V = \operatorname{Sing}(\widehat X_p)$ if $p\mid \bm{v}$.
If $p\nmid\bm{v}$ and $[\overline{\bm{v}}]\notin \mathcal W_{t,p}(\mathbb{F}_p)$,
then $\dim V \leqslant \dim \Gamma_{p,[\overline{\bm{v}}]} \leqslant t-1$,
by the analogue of \eqref{EQ:smooth-sing-containment} over $\mathbb{F}_p$.
Thus \eqref{eq:p2-strat-bound} follows.
Moreover, Theorem~\ref{Thm: ZaksBoundSingLocus} implies
$\dim V \leqslant \dim \operatorname{Sing}(X_p \cap \{\overline{\bm{v}}\cdot\bm{x}=0\})
\leqslant \dim \operatorname{Sing}(X_p) + 1
\leqslant n-5$ if $p\nmid \bm{v}$.
If $p\mid\bm{v}$,
then $\dim V = 1 + \dim \operatorname{Sing}(X_p) \leqslant n-5$.
Either way, \eqref{eq:p2-cutoff} follows.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{Bernert-n10-sing-series}
If $n\geqslant 10$ and $F$ is good,
then $\mathfrak S := \sum_{q\geqslant 1} q^{-n} S_q(\bm0)$
converges absolutely to a positive real number,
and satisfies
\[
\mathfrak S=\prod_p\chi_p,
\]
where
\[
\chi_p
:=\sum_{k\geqslant0}p^{-kn}S_{p^k}(\bm0)
=\lim_{j\to\infty}p^{-j(n-1)}
\#\{\bm{x}\bmod p^j:F(\bm{x})\equiv0\bmod p^j\}
>0.
\]
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
This follows from \cite[\S2, Theorem~1]{Ber25}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{LEM:max-G-multiplicative}
The quantity $\mathcal G_{A,T}(\bm{y})$ is multiplicative in $T$.
That is,
\begin{equation}
\label{EQ:max-G-multiplicative}
\mathcal G_{A,T_1T_2}(\bm{y})
= \mathcal G_{A,T_1}(\bm{y})
\mathcal G_{A,T_2}(\bm{y})
\end{equation}
for all $A,T_1,T_2\geqslant 1$ with $\gcd(T_1,T_2)=1$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{LEM:max-G-A-invariant}
As a function of $\bm{y}$,
the quantity $\mathcal G_{A,T}(\bm{y})$
only depends on $\bm{y} \bmod{\gcd(A,T)}$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:q-flexible-lifting}
Let $A,T\geqslant 1$ and $q = A^2T$.
Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:q-flexible-pointwise}
|S_q(\bm{v})|
\leqslant A^{n+1} T
\sum_{a\in (\mathbb{Z}/A\mathbb{Z})^\ast}
\sum_{\substack{\bm{y}\bmod A\\F(\bm{y})\equiv0\bmod A
\\ a\nabla F(\bm{y})+\bm{v}\equiv \bm0\bmod A}} \mathcal G_{A,T}(\bm{y}).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Let
\begin{equation}
\label{z-sum-in-max-G}
\mathcal{S}_{A,T}(\bm{d},\alpha,\bm{y})
:= \sum_{\bm{z}\bmod T} e_T(\bm{d}\cdot\bm{z}+\alpha Q_{\bm{y}}(\bm{z})+\alpha A F(\bm{z}))
\end{equation}
be the $\bm{z}$-sum in \eqref{eq:GAT-max-sum}.
If $\gcd(T_1,T_2)=1$,
the Chinese remainder theorem implies
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{S}_{A,T_1T_2}(\bm{d},\alpha,\bm{y})
= \mathcal{S}_{A,T_1}(\overline{T_2}\bm{d},\overline{T_2}\alpha,\bm{y})
\mathcal{S}_{A,T_2}(\overline{T_1}\bm{d},\overline{T_1}\alpha,\bm{y}).
\end{equation*}
By the Chinese remainder theorem, the pairs
$(\overline{T_2}\bm{d},\overline{T_2}\alpha)\bmod T_1$
and
$(\overline{T_1}\bm{d},\overline{T_1}\alpha)\bmod T_2$
range independently over their respective parameter sets.
Thus the two local maxima can be attained simultaneously,
and taking the maximum of the absolute value gives the
claimed equality.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
The definition gives $T$-periodicity in $\bm{y}$.
To prove $A$-periodicity, put
$$
P_{\bm{y}}(\bm{z}):=Q_{\bm{y}}(\bm{z})+AF(\bm{z}).
$$
For $\bm{h}\in\mathbb{Z}^n$, Taylor expansion gives
$$
P_{\bm{y}+A\bm{h}}(\bm{z})
=P_{\bm{y}}(\bm{z}+\bm{h})
-\boldsymbol{\ell}\cdot\bm{z}-P_{\bm{y}}(\bm{h}),
$$
where
$\boldsymbol{\ell}:=H(\bm{y})\bm{h}+A\nabla F(\bm{h})$.
Translating the summation variable in
\eqref{z-sum-in-max-G} therefore gives
$$
|\mathcal S_{A,T}(\bm{d},\alpha,\bm{y}+A\bm{h})|
=
|\mathcal S_{A,T}(\bm{d}-\alpha\boldsymbol{\ell},
\alpha,\bm{y})|.
$$
For each $\alpha$, the map
$\bm{d}\mapsto\bm{d}-\alpha\boldsymbol{\ell}$
is a bijection modulo $T$.
Taking maxima proves
$\mathcal G_{A,T}(\bm{y}+A\bm{h})=\mathcal G_{A,T}(\bm{y})$.
Together with $T$-periodicity, this gives the desired
$\gcd(A,T)$-periodicity.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Let \(M:=AT\).
Then \(q=A^2T=AM\),
$\operatorname{rad}(q)=\operatorname{rad}(AT)=\operatorname{rad}(M)$,
and $M^2=A^2T^2=qT\equiv 0\bmod{q}$.
For $a,\bm{x}$ as in \eqref{eq:defSq},
write
\[
 \bm{x}=\bm{x}_0+M\bm{h}_0,\qquad
 a=a_0+Me,
\]
with $0\leqslant \bm{x}_0<M$ and $0\leqslant a_0<M$
running over a complete set of representatives modulo $M$,
and similarly with $0\leqslant \bm{h}_0<A$ and $0\leqslant e<A$.
Since \(\operatorname{rad}(M)=\operatorname{rad}(q)\),
the condition $\gcd(a,q)=1$ is equivalent to $\gcd(a_0,M)=1$.
Taylor expansion of $F(\bm{x}_0+M\bm{h}_0)$ gives
\begin{equation*}
a F(\bm{x})+\bm{v}\cdot\bm{x}
\equiv (a_0+Me) F(\bm{x}_0) + a_0 M\nabla F(\bm{x}_0)\cdot\bm{h}_0
+ \bm{v}\cdot(\bm{x}_0+M\bm{h}_0) \bmod{q},
\end{equation*}
since $M^2 \equiv 0\bmod{q}$.
Orthogonality in \(e,\bm{h}_0\bmod{A}\) gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:q-first-lift}
S_q(\bm{v})=A^{n+1}
\sum_{\substack{0\leqslant a_0<M \\ \gcd(a_0,M)=1}}
\sum_{\substack{0\leqslant \bm{x}_0<M\\
F(\bm{x}_0)\equiv 0\bmod{A}\\
a_0\nabla F(\bm{x}_0)+\bm{v}\equiv \bm0\bmod{A}}}
e_q(a_0 F(\bm{x}_0)+\bm{v}\cdot\bm{x}_0).
\end{equation}
For all $\bm{x}_0$ in the support of \eqref{eq:q-first-lift},
write \(\bm{x}_0=\bm{y}+A\bm{z}\), with
$0\leqslant \bm{y}<A$ and $0\leqslant \bm{z}<T$.
Then $$\bm{d} := \frac{a_0\nabla F(\bm{y})+\bm{v}}{A} \in \mathbb{Z}^n,$$
since $a_0\nabla F(\bm{x}_0)+\bm{v}\equiv \bm0\bmod{A}$.
Taylor expansion of $F(\bm{y}+A\bm{z})$ gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\frac{e_q(a_0 F(\bm{x}_0)+\bm{v}\cdot\bm{x}_0)}{e_q(a_0 F(\bm{y}) + \bm{v}\cdot\bm{y})}
&= e_q(a_0 A\nabla F(\bm{y})\cdot\bm{z}
+ a_0 A^2Q_{\bm{y}}(\bm{z}) + a_0 A^3F(\bm{z})
+ A\bm{v}\cdot \bm{z}) \\
&= e_T(\bm{d}\cdot\bm{z}+a_0 Q_{\bm{y}}(\bm{z})+a_0 A F(\bm{z}))
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
in view of the identity $e_q(A^2x) = e_{A^2T}(A^2x) = e_T(x)$.
By the triangle inequality on \eqref{eq:q-first-lift},
\begin{equation*}
|S_q(\bm{v})|
\leqslant A^{n+1}
\sum_{\substack{0\leqslant a_0<M \\ \gcd(a_0,M)=1}}
\sum_{\substack{0\leqslant \bm{y}<A\\
F(\bm{y})\equiv 0\bmod{A}\\
a_0\nabla F(\bm{y})+\bm{v}\equiv \bm0\bmod{A}}}
|\mathcal{S}_{A,T}(\bm{d},a_0,\bm{y})|,
\end{equation*}
where $\mathcal{S}_{A,T}$ was defined in \eqref{z-sum-in-max-G}.
By definition, $|\mathcal{S}_{A,T}|
\leqslant \mathcal G_{A,T}(\bm{y})$.
Since $\mathcal G_{A,T}(\bm{y})$ is independent of $a_0$,
and the condition $a_0\nabla F(\bm{y})+\bm{v}\equiv \bm0\bmod{A}$
depends only on $a_0\bmod{A}$,
the desired inequality \eqref{eq:q-flexible-pointwise} follows
from the fact that each fibre of the map $(\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z})^\ast \to (\mathbb{Z}/A\mathbb{Z})^\ast$
has cardinality $\varphi(M)/\varphi(A)
= \varphi(AT)/\varphi(A) \leqslant T$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{Bernert-Smith-bound}
Let $r(\bm{a})$ be the rank of $H(\bm{a})$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
Then $N_d(\bm{a}) \ll_F d^{n-r(\bm{a})} |\bm{a}|^{r(\bm{a})}$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
This is \cite[Eq.~(3.1)]{Ber25},
applied to the cubic form $C := 6F$.
It does not require goodness.
For $C=6F$,
Bernert's notation $M,\bm{h},q$ corresponds to our notation $H,\bm{a},d$,
and his bilinear forms $B_i(\bm{x},\bm{y})$
are simply the entries of the vector $M(\bm{x})\bm{y} = H(\bm{x})\bm{y}$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{LEM:square-and-diff}
If $A,T\geqslant 1$ are integers with $T\mid A$, then
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal G_{A,T}(\bm{a})
\leqslant T^{n/2} N_T(\bm{a})^{1/2}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Since $T\mid A$,
the definition of $\mathcal G_{A,T}$ in \eqref{eq:GAT-max-sum} simplifies to
\[
\mathcal G_{A,T}(\bm{a})
= \max_{\substack{\alpha\in (\mathbb{Z}/T\mathbb{Z})^\ast\\
\bm{d}\in (\mathbb{Z}/T\mathbb{Z})^n}}
\left|
\sum_{\bm{z}\in (\mathbb{Z}/T\mathbb{Z})^n}
e_T(\bm{d}\cdot\bm{z}+\alpha Q_{\bm{a}}(\bm{z}))
\right|,
\]
where $Q_{\bm{a}}(\bm{z}):=\frac12\bm{z}^tH(\bm{a})\bm{z}$.
On squaring and differencing the $\bm{z}$-sum, exactly as in the close of the proof of
\cite[Lemma~11]{41}, we are led to the desired conclusion.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:c/d-bound}
Let $c,d$ be positive integers such that $d$ is square-free and $d\mid c$.
Let $\bm{k}\in \mathbb{Z}^n$ such that $d\mid F(\bm{k})$. 
Then
$$
\#\left\{ \bm{x}\in (\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z})^n: 
\begin{array}{l}
\bm{x}\equiv \bm{k}\bmod{d}\\
F(\bm{x})\equiv 0\bmod{c}
\end{array}
\right\}\ll \left(\frac{c}{d}\right)^{n-1+\varepsilon} 
\gcd(d_2,\nabla F(\bm{k}))\gcd(d_2,\bm{k}),
$$
for any $\varepsilon>0$, where $d_2=d/d_1$ and $d_1$ is defined in \eqref{Defi:d1}.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Let $N(c,d)$ be the quantity to be counted in the lemma.
By the Chinese remainder theorem, it suffices to treat the case where
$c=p^\ell$ and $d=p^j$, where $j\in\{0,1\}$ and $\ell\geqslant j$.
If $j=0$, additive orthogonality gives
\begin{equation*}
N(p^\ell,1)
= p^{-\ell} \sum_{1\leqslant a\leqslant p^\ell} \sum_{\bm{x}\bmod{p^\ell}} e_{p^\ell}(aF(\bm{x}))
= p^{-\ell} \sum_{h=0}^\ell p^{(\ell-h)n}S_{p^h}(\bm0)
= p^{(n-1)\ell} \sum_{h=0}^\ell p^{-hn}S_{p^h}(\bm0)
\end{equation*}
where $h = \ell - v_p(a)$.
Thus $N(p^\ell,1)
\leqslant p^{(n-1)\ell} \sum_{q\geqslant 1} q^{-n} |S_q(\bm0)|
\ll_F p^{(n-1)\ell}$
by \eqref{Bernert-n10-absolute}.

Suppose $j=1$.
For $\ell=1$ we have $N(p,p)=1$.
Now suppose $\ell\geqslant 2$.
For any fixed prime $p$ we have
$N(p^\ell,p) \leqslant N(p^\ell,1)
\ll_F p^{(n-1)\ell} \ll_p p^{(n-1)(\ell-1)}$.
At every other prime we have $p>3$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-two-on-cubic}
F(\bm u)=0,\quad \bm u\in \overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^n \setminus \{\bm0\}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{rank}H(\bm u)\geqslant2,
\end{equation}
by spreading out the claim $V_1 \cap \widehat X = \{\bm0\}$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:hesrank}.

If $p\mid\bm k$, homogeneity gives
$N(p^2,p) = p^n = p^{(\ell-1)(n-1)+1}$ for $\ell=2$, and
\[
N(p^\ell,p)=p^{2n}N(p^{\ell-3},1)
\ll_F p^{2+2(n-1)} p^{(\ell-3)(n-1)}
= p^{(\ell-1)(n-1)+2}
\]
for $\ell\geqslant3$.
If $p\nmid \bm k$ and $p\nmid\nabla F(\bm k)$, Hensel lifting gives
$N(p^\ell,p) = p^{(\ell-1)(n-1)}$.

It remains to consider the case where $p\nmid\bm k$ and $p\mid\nabla F(\bm k)$.
Write $\bm x=\bm k+p\bm y$.
If $p^2\nmid F(\bm k)$,
then $N(p^\ell,p)=0$ for all $\ell\geqslant 2$.
Now suppose $p^2\mid F(\bm k)$.
Then
\[
p^{-2}F(\bm k+p\bm y)
=p^{-2}F(\bm k)+p^{-1}\nabla F(\bm k)\cdot\bm y
+\tfrac12\bm y^tH(\bm k)\bm y+pF(\bm y)
\in \mathbb{Z}_p[\bm{y}].
\]
Here $\operatorname{rank} H(\bm k \bmod{p}) \geqslant 2$ by \eqref{eq:rank-two-on-cubic}.
Applying Lemma~\ref{LEM:rank-two-root-lifting}
with $s=\ell-2\geqslant 0$ therefore gives
\[
N(p^\ell,p) = p^n \#\{\bm{y}\bmod{p^s}: p^{-2}F(\bm k+p\bm y) \equiv 0\bmod{p^s}\}
\leqslant p^n (\ell-1)p^{(\ell-2)(n-1)}.
\]
This is satisfactory, since $\ell-1 \ll p^{(\ell-1)\varepsilon}$
and $p^n p^{(\ell-2)(n-1)} = p^{(\ell-1)(n-1) + 1}$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{LEM:rank-two-root-lifting}
Suppose $p$ is odd.
Let $f_i\in \mathbb{Z}_p[\bm{y}]$ be homogeneous of degree $i$, for $0\leqslant i\leqslant 3$.
Suppose $\operatorname{rank}(f_2\bmod{p}) \geqslant 2$.
Let $g:=f_0+f_1+f_2+pf_3$.
Then, for every $s\geqslant0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-two-root-lifting}
\#\{\bm y\bmod p^s:g(\bm y)\equiv0\bmod p^s\}
\leqslant (s+1)p^{s(n-1)}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Since $p\ne 2$, we may diagonalise the quadratic form $f_2$ over $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
After permuting coordinates if necessary, we can
assume the coefficients are listed in increasing order of valuation.
Then $f_2 = \sum_{1\leqslant i\leqslant n} c_iy_i^2$
with $n\geqslant 2$ and $v_p(c_1)=v_p(c_2)=0$, say.
Fix $y_3,\ldots,y_n$ modulo $p^s$. After collecting homogeneous
terms in $y_1,y_2$, the resulting binary polynomial again has
the form $h_0+h_1+h_2+ph_3$, with each $h_i$ homogeneous of
degree $i$, and
$h_2\equiv c_1y_1^2+c_2y_2^2\bmod p$.
Thus its quadratic part has rank two modulo $p$. The binary
case of the lemma gives at most $(s+1)p^s$ solutions for each
of the $p^{s(n-2)}$ choices of the remaining variables,
proving the required bound.


For $n=2$, we induct on $s\geqslant 0$.
If $s\leqslant 1$ the bound \eqref{eq:rank-two-root-lifting} is well known, so assume $s\geqslant 2$.
Suppose again that $f_2 = c_1y_1^2+c_2y_2^2$.
By completing the square, we may assume that $p\mid f_1$.
If $p\nmid f_0$, then $g\equiv 0\bmod{p}$ is a smooth affine conic,
so $\#\{\bm{y}\in \mathbb{F}_p^2: g=0\} \leqslant p+1 \leqslant (s+1)p$,
and \eqref{eq:rank-two-root-lifting} holds by Hensel's lemma.
If $p\mid f_0$, then $g\equiv 0\bmod{p}$ is smooth away from the origin.
The contribution to \eqref{eq:rank-two-root-lifting} from $\bm{y}\equiv \bm0\bmod{p}$
is zero unless $p^2\mid f_0$, in which case it
is at most $p^2 (s-1)p^{s-2}$, by the $s-2$ case of \eqref{eq:rank-two-root-lifting}
for the polynomial
$$p^{-2} g(p\bm{z}) = p^{-2}f_0 + p^{-1}f_1(\bm{z}) + f_2(\bm{z}) + p^2f_3(\bm{z}).$$
The contribution to \eqref{eq:rank-two-root-lifting} from $\bm{y}\not\equiv \bm0\bmod{p}$
is at most $p^{s-1} (1+1)p$, by Hensel's lemma and
the $s=1$ case of \eqref{eq:rank-two-root-lifting}.
Adding the two contributions gives \eqref{eq:rank-two-root-lifting}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{LEM:weighted-rank-locus}
If $0\leqslant \varrho\leqslant n$, then
$$\sum_{\substack{\bm u\in\mathbb{F}_p^n\\F(\bm u)=0\\
\operatorname{rank} H(\bm u) = \varrho}}
\gcd(p,\nabla F(\bm u))\gcd(p,\bm u)
\ll_F p^{\delta_n(\varrho) + \gamma_n(\varrho)}.$$
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
The case $\varrho=0$ is immediate from \eqref{eq:q-first-rank},
since $\delta_n(0)=0 \leqslant n-5$ and $\gamma_n(0)=2$.
Now suppose $\varrho\geqslant 1$.
Then $H(\bm u)$ is nonzero, so $\bm u\not\equiv \bm0 \bmod{p}$ and $\gcd(p,\bm u) = 1$.
The case $\gamma_n(\varrho)\geqslant 1$ is then immediate from \eqref{eq:q-first-rank}.
Finally, suppose $\gamma_n(\varrho)=0$.
Then $\delta_n(\varrho)\geqslant n-4$ by \eqref{eq:q-gamma}.
In view of \eqref{eq:n10-sing-X}, the Lang--Weil estimate gives
$$\#\{\bm u\bmod{p}: \nabla F(\bm u) \equiv 0\bmod{p}\} \ll_F p^{n-5}
\leqslant p^{\delta_n(\varrho)-1}.$$
On the other hand, there are $\ll p^{\delta_n(\varrho)}$ smooth residues $\bm u$ at hand, by \eqref{eq:q-first-rank}.
After multiplying by $\gcd(p,\nabla F(\bm u))$,
we find that both the singular and smooth contributions are satisfactory.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:starT}
Let $r=c^2d$ be squarefull. Then 
$$
|S_r(\bm{v})|\leqslant 
c^{n+1}d^{n/2+1}
\sum_{a\in (\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z})^*} \sum_{
\substack{\bm{a}\in (\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z})^n\\ 
c\mid F(\bm{a})\\
c\mid (a\nabla F(\bm{a})+\bm{v})}} N_d(\bm{a})^{1/2},
$$
where $N_d(\bm{a})$ is given by \eqref{eq:N_d}.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Apply Lemmas~\ref{lem:q-flexible-lifting} and~\ref{LEM:square-and-diff}
with $A := c$ and $T := d$, using the fact that $d\mid c$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:frog}
We have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-prime-smith-mass}
\sum_{\substack{\bm u\in\mathbb{F}_p^n\\F(\bm u)=0}}
N_p(\bm u)^{1/2}
\gcd(p,\nabla F(\bm u))\gcd(p,\bm u)
\ll_F p^{3n/2 - \lceil n/3\rceil - 1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{LEM:weighted-rank-locus} bounds the left-hand side by
$\sum_{0\leqslant \varrho\leqslant n} p^{\delta_n(\varrho) + \gamma_n(\varrho)} p^{(n-\varrho)/2}$.
For $\varrho\geqslant 2\lceil n/3\rceil$,
we have $\delta_n(\varrho) = n-1$ and $\gamma_n(\varrho) = 0$, so
\begin{equation*}
\delta_n(\varrho)+\gamma_n(\varrho)
+\frac{n-\varrho}{2}
= n-1 + \frac{n-\varrho}{2}
\leqslant \frac{3n}{2}-\lceil n/3\rceil-1.
\end{equation*}
For $\varrho=0$, we have $\delta_n(\varrho)=0$ and $\gamma_n(\varrho)=2$,
so $\delta_n(\varrho)+\gamma_n(\varrho) + (n-\varrho)/2
= 2 + n/2 \leqslant 3n/2 - \lceil n/3\rceil - 1$,
since $n\geqslant 10$.
For $1\leqslant\varrho<2\lceil n/3\rceil$, definitions
\eqref{eq:q-delta} and \eqref{eq:q-gamma} give
\[
\delta_n(\varrho)-\varrho\leqslant \lfloor n/3\rfloor - 1,
\qquad
\delta_n(\varrho)+2\gamma_n(\varrho)
= \delta_n(\varrho) + 2\cdot \bm{1}_{\delta_n(\varrho)\leqslant n-5} \leqslant n-2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta_n(\varrho)+\gamma_n(\varrho)+\frac{n-\varrho}{2}
&=\frac n2+
\frac{\delta_n(\varrho)-\varrho}{2}
+\frac{\delta_n(\varrho)+2\gamma_n(\varrho)}{2}\\
&\leqslant n+\frac{\lfloor n/3\rfloor-3}{2}\\
&\leqslant\frac{3n}{2}-\lceil n/3\rceil-1,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last inequality follows from
$\lfloor n/3\rfloor+2\lceil n/3\rceil\leqslant n+1$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:cube-sum1}
Let $d\mid c$ with $d$ square-free.
We have
\[
L_1(c,d,\mathcal V)
\ll_{F,\varepsilon}
c^{2n+1+\varepsilon}d^{n-\lceil n/3\rceil+1}E_c(\mathcal V).
\]
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Interchanging the sums in \eqref{Eq: Defi.Lc,d,V} gives
\[
L_1(c,d,\mathcal V)
\leqslant c^{n+2}d^{n/2+1}E_c(\mathcal V)
\sum_{\substack{\bm a\bmod c\\c\mid F(\bm a)}}N_d(\bm a)^{1/2}.
\]
Splitting the last sum into residue classes modulo $d$ and applying
Lemma~\ref{lem:c/d-bound} shows that it is at most
\[
\ll_{F,\varepsilon}(c/d)^{n-1+\varepsilon}
\sum_{\substack{\bm u\bmod d\\d\mid F(\bm u)}}
N_d(\bm u)^{1/2}
\gcd(d_2,\nabla F(\bm u))\gcd(d_2,\bm u).
\]
By the Chinese remainder theorem and Lemma~\ref{lem:frog}, the last
sum is $\ll_{F,\varepsilon}d^{3n/2 - \lceil n/3\rceil - 1+\varepsilon}$.
Combining these estimates proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:onion}
Let $r=c^2d$, where $d\mid c$ is square-free, and let
$\mathcal V\subset\mathbb{Z}^n\cap(\bm{v}_0+[-V,V]^n)$, with $V\geqslant1$.
Uniformly in $\bm{v}_0\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we have
\[
 \sum_{\bm{v}\in\mathcal V}|S_r(\bm{v})|
 \leqslant L_1(c,d,\mathcal V)
 \ll_{F,\varepsilon}
 r^{n/2+1+\varepsilon}d_1^{a_n}d_2^{b_n}(V+r^{1/3})^n.
\]
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
The first inequality is \eqref{eq:from-lemstar}.
On replacing the box radius by $V+r^{1/3}$,
the second inequality reduces to the claim
\[
 L_1(c,d,\mathcal V)
 \ll_{F,\varepsilon}r^{n/2+1+\varepsilon}d_1^{a_n}d_2^{b_n}V^n
 \qquad(V\geqslant r^{1/3}).
\]
We henceforth assume $V\geqslant r^{1/3}$.
If $c\leqslant V$, then $E_c(\mathcal V)\ll(V/c)^n$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:cube-sum1} gives
\begin{align*}
L_1(c,d,\mathcal V)
&\ll_{F,\varepsilon}c^{n+1+\varepsilon}d^{n-\lceil n/3\rceil+1}V^n\\
&= r^{n/2+1}c^\varepsilon\frac dc\,d^{a_n}V^n
\leqslant r^{n/2+1+\varepsilon}d_1^{a_n}d_2^{b_n}V^n,
\end{align*}
since $d/c\leqslant 1$, $d=d_1d_2$, and $a_n\leqslant b_n$.
We may therefore assume $c>V$.

Two auxiliary results will be useful.
First, for integers $m\geqslant1$ and real $R\geqslant1$,
Lemma~\ref{Bernert-Smith-bound} and goodness
(Definition~\ref{defn : good}) give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:good-kernel-average}
\sum_{|\bm{h}|\leqslant R}N_m(\bm{h})^{1/2}
\ll_{F,\varepsilon}m^{n/2}R^\varepsilon \sum_{j=0}^n(R^3/m)^{j/2}
\ll_n R^\varepsilon m^{n/2}(1+R^3/m)^{n/2}.
\end{equation}
Second, 
on recalling the definition \eqref{eq:N_d}
of $N_p(\bm{u})$, it follows from combining 
the incidence bound \eqref{EQ:clean-slop-incidence-bound}
 with the Lang--Weil estimate, that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:laval_dim}
 \sum_{\bm{u}\in\mathbb{F}_p^n}N_p(\bm{u})
 \ll_F p^{n+\lfloor n/3\rfloor-1}.
\end{equation}

In the nonnegative sum \eqref{Eq: Defi.Lc,d,V}
defining $L_1(c,d,\mathcal V)$, we may weaken $c\mid F(\bm{a})$
to $d_1\mid F(\bm{a})$, and majorise the box $\bm{v}_0+[-V,V]^n$ by the
