\left|\int_{|t|<B_q}p_q(t/P^3)J_w(t)\,\mathrm{d} t-\int_{\mathbb{R}} J_w(t) \,\mathrm{d} t\right|
&\leqslant\int_{|t|<B_q}|p_q(t/P^3)-1|\,|J_w(t)|\,\mathrm{d} t
+\int_{|t|\geqslant B_q}|J_w(t)|\,\mathrm{d} t\\
&\ll_w \frac qQ\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+|t|)^4|J_w(t)|\,\mathrm{d} t+B_q^{-1}
\ll_{F,w}\frac qQ,
\end{align*}
where we have applied the $N=1$ case of \eqref{eq:MV-kernel-estimate},
together with the rapid decay of $J_w$.
Consequently, by the triangle inequality
and the absolute convergence of $\mathfrak S_\Omega$
from Lemma~\ref{LEM:localised-singular-series-convergence},
\begin{align*}
\frac{M(P)}{P^{n-3}}-\mathfrak S_\Omega \int_{\mathbb{R}} J_w(t) \,\mathrm{d} t
&\ll_{F,w}\sum_{q\leqslant Q}\frac{|S_{q,W}(\bm{0})|}{\operatorname{lcm}(q,W)^n} \frac qQ
+\sum_{q>Q} \frac{|S_{q,W}(\bm{0})|}{\operatorname{lcm}(q,W)^n} \int_{\mathbb{R}} J_w(t) \,\mathrm{d} t \\
& \ll Q^{-1/2} \sum_{q\geqslant 1} \frac{|S_{q,W}(\bm{0})|}{\operatorname{lcm}(q,W)^n}
+ \sum_{q>Q^{1/2}} \frac{|S_{q,W}(\bm{0})|}{\operatorname{lcm}(q,W)^n} = o(1)
\end{align*}
as $P\to \infty$.
Thus $M(P)/P^{n-3} \to \mathfrak S_\Omega \int_{\mathbb{R}} J_w(t) \,\mathrm{d} t > 0$,
as $P\to \infty$, where the positivity of $\mathfrak{S}_\Omega$ is a consequence of Lemma~\ref{LEM:localised-singular-series-convergence}.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- lemma-47: body_md -->
\label{lem:gradient-volume}
Let $q\asymp_W R$, $|\theta|\sim \phi$, and let $V_0$ be given by \eqref{eq:V}.
Assume that \eqref{eq:diffU} holds.
Then, for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every
$\bm{v}\in \mathbb{R}^n$, we have
\[
\operatorname{Vol}\left\{
\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n:
|\bm{x}/P-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant 2\ell,\;
|q\theta\nabla F(\bm{x})-\bm{v}|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0
\right\}
\ll
P^{n+O_n(\varepsilon)}\left(\frac{R}{PV_0}\right)^{\rho},
\]
where $\rho=r(F)$.
<!-- end lemma-47 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
We may assume that $\theta \neq 0$, since $\phi>0$.
Write $\bm{x}=P\bm{y}$.
As $F$ is cubic, we have
$\nabla F(P\bm{y})=P^2\nabla F(\bm{y})$ and the volume in question is
\[
P^n\operatorname{Vol}\left\{
\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n:
|\bm{y}-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant 2\ell,\;
|q\theta P^2\nabla F(\bm{y})-\bm{v}|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0
\right\}.
\]
By \eqref{eq:diffU}, the box $|\bm{y}-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant 2\ell$ is contained in $U$.
Using the diffeomorphism
$$\bm{y}\mapsto (\Psi(\bm{y}),y_{\rho+1},\dots,y_n)$$
on $U$ and the Jacobian bound \eqref{eq:smoothsub''},
where $\Psi$ was defined in \eqref{eq:Psi},
we find by Fubini's theorem that
\[
\operatorname{Vol}\{\bm{y}\in U:|\Psi(\bm{y})-\bm{a}|\leqslant \Delta\}
\ll \Delta^\rho ,
\]
uniformly for $\bm{a}\in\mathbb{R}^\rho$ and $0<\Delta\leqslant 1$.
For $\Delta>1$ we take the trivial bound $O(1)$ for the volume. 
It follows that
\begin{equation}
\label{preslop}
\operatorname{Vol}\left\{
\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n:
|\bm{y}-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant 2\ell,\;
|\nabla F(\bm{y})-\bm{b}|\leqslant \Delta
\right\}
\ll \min\{1,\Delta^\rho\},
\end{equation}
uniformly 
for $\bm{b}\in\mathbb{R}^n$.


Applying this with $\bm{b}=(q\theta P^2)^{-1}\bm{v}$ and 
$\Delta= (q|\theta|P^2 )^{-1}P^\varepsilon V_0$, we deduce that 
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Vol}\left\{
\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n:
|\bm{x}/P-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant 2\ell,\;
|q\theta\nabla F(\bm{x})-\bm{v}|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0
\right\}
\ll 
P^{n+O_n(\varepsilon)}
\min\left\{
1,
\frac{ V_0}{R\phi P^2}
\right\}^\rho,
\end{equation*}
since $q\asymp_W R$ and $|\theta|\sim\phi$. The lemma will follow if we are able to show that 
$$
\min\left\{
1,
\frac{ V_0}{R\phi P^2}\right\}
\ll \frac{R}{PV_0},
$$
where we recall that $V_0$ is given by \eqref{eq:V}. 
But this is easily checked on a case distinction between 
the case  $\phi P^3\leqslant 1$ (so that $V_0=RP^{-1}$) and the case
 $\phi P^3>1$ (so that $V_0=RP^{-1}\sqrt{\phi P^3}$).
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- lemma-48: body_md -->
\label{lem:gradient-volume2}
Let $q\asymp_W R$, $|\theta|\sim \phi$, and let $V, V_0$ be given by \eqref{eq:V}.
Then, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
we have
\[
\sum_{\substack{\bm{v}\in \mathbb{Z}^n\\ 
|\bm{v}|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V}}
\operatorname{Vol}\left\{
\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n:
|\bm{x}/P-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant 2\ell,\;
|q\theta\nabla F(\bm{x})-\bm{v}|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0
\right\}
\ll
P^{n+O_n(\varepsilon)}(1+V_0)^n.
\]
<!-- end lemma-48 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
Interchanging the integral with the sum, we are left with estimating the number of  integer vectors $\bm{v}$, each of whose entries lie in an interval of length $O(P^\varepsilon V_0)$. The statement of the lemma is now clear,
on integrating over $\bm{x}$ such that $|\bm{x}/P-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant 2\ell$.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- lemma-49: body_md -->
\label{aislop}
Fix $\varepsilon>0$.
Let $P,R\geqslant 1/2$ and $\phi>0$.
Let $V,V_0$ be given by \eqref{eq:V}.
Assume that \eqref{eq:diffU} holds.
Let $\rho=r(F)$.
Let $L\geqslant 0$ be a real number.
If $|\alpha| \asymp_W R\phi$, then
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{\bm{v}\in \mathbb{Z}^n}
M_\alpha(\bm{v},L) \ll
\begin{cases}       
0 &\text{ if $P^\varepsilon V < 1$,}\\
P^{n+O_n(\varepsilon)} (1+\tfrac{L}{V})^\rho (1+V_0+L)^{n-\rho} V_0^\rho & \text{ if $\phi P^3>1$},\\
P^{n+O_n(\varepsilon)} (V+L)^n & \text{ if $\phi P^3\leqslant 1$},
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
where
\begin{equation*}
M_\alpha(\bm{v},L) := \sup_{\substack{\bm{a}\in \mathbb{Z}^n\\ 
0<|\bm{a}|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V\\
|\bm{a}-\bm{v}| \leqslant L}}
\operatorname{Vol}\left\{
\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n:
|\bm{x}/P-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant 2\ell,\;
|\alpha\nabla F(\bm{x})-\bm{a}|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0
\right\},
\end{equation*}
with the convention that $\sup_{\emptyset} = 0$
if the set in the supremum is empty.
<!-- end lemma-49 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
For each $\bm{v}$
for which the set in the supremum is nonempty,
choose $\bm{a}=\bm{a}(\bm{v})$
with $0<|\bm{a}|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V$
and $|\bm{a}-\bm{v}| \leqslant L$
such that
\begin{equation}
\label{choose-shifted box-max-vector-a}
M_\alpha(\bm{v},L) =
\operatorname{Vol}\left\{
\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n:
|\bm{x}/P-\bm{x}_0|\leqslant 2\ell,\;
|\alpha\nabla F(\bm{x})-\bm{a}|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0
\right\}.
\end{equation}
In particular, the outer sum is zero unless $P^\varepsilon V \geqslant 1$, which we now assume.
We begin as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:gradient-volume} by writing $\bm{x}=P\bm{y}$,
where $\bm{y}\in U$ by \eqref{eq:diffU}.
By the discussion after \eqref{eq:Psi},
we have a diffeomorphism
\begin{equation}
\label{key-diffeomorphism}
U\xrightarrow{\cong} S\subset \mathbb{R}^n, \quad 
\bm{y} \mapsto \left(\Psi(\bm{y}),y_{\rho+1},\dots,y_n\right),
\end{equation}
for which the Jacobian and the  Jacobian of the inverse map are uniformly bounded on $U$.
Then, for all vectors $\bm{s},\bm{t}\in \mathbb{R}^\rho$ and $\bm{y}''\in \mathbb{R}^{n-\rho}$
with $(\bm{s},\bm{y}''),(\bm{t},\bm{y}'')\in U$, we have
\begin{align}
|\nabla F(\bm{s},\bm{y}'') - \nabla F(\bm{t},\bm{y}'')|
&\ll_U |\bm{s}-\bm{t}|,
\label{easy-grad-smooth} \\
|\Psi(\bm{s},\bm{y}'') - \Psi(\bm{t},\bm{y}'')|
&\gg_U |\bm{s}-\bm{t}|.
\label{inverse-lipschitz-Psi}
\end{align}
The inequality \eqref{easy-grad-smooth} is a general consequence of the smoothness of $\nabla F$;
the inequality \eqref{inverse-lipschitz-Psi} similarly follows from the smoothness of the inverse of the diffeomorphism \eqref{key-diffeomorphism}.

Let us write $\bm{v}=(\bm{v}',\bm{v}'')$
and $\bm{a}=(\bm{a}',\bm{a}'')$
for $\bm{v}',\bm{a}'\in \mathbb{Z}^\rho$ and $\bm{v}'',\bm{a}''\in \mathbb{Z}^{n-\rho}$.
Similarly write $\bm{y}=(\bm{y}',\bm{y}'')$,
where $\bm{y}'\in \mathbb{R}^\rho$ and $\bm{y}''\in \mathbb{R}^{n-\rho}$.
By the triangle inequality
$$|\alpha\nabla F(\bm{x})-\bm{v}|
\leqslant |\alpha\nabla F(\bm{x})-\bm{a}| + |\bm{a}-\bm{v}|
\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0 + L$$
and the change of coordinates $\bm{x}=P\bm{y}$,
\begin{equation}
\label{drop-L-box}
\operatorname{Vol}\left\{
\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n:
\bm{x}/P\in U,\;
|\alpha\nabla F(\bm{x})-\bm{a}|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0
\right\}
\leqslant P^n \int_{\substack{\bm{y}\in U\\
|\alpha P^2\Psi(\bm{y})-\bm{a}'|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0}}
\bm{1}_{A(\bm{y},\bm{v})}\,
\mathrm{d}\bm{y},
\end{equation}
where $A(\bm{y},\bm{v})$ denotes the condition that
$|\alpha P^2 \frac{\partial F(\bm{y})}{\partial y_j}  
-v_j|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0 + L$ for $1\leqslant j\leqslant n$.
The condition $A(\bm{y},\bm{v})$ constrains $\bm{v}$ directly,
rather than $\bm{a}$,
at the cost of introducing a summand $L$.
If $\bm{v}'$ and $\bm{y}''$ are fixed,
then any two possible choices $\bm{s},\bm{t}\in \mathbb{R}^\rho$ for the vector
$\bm{y}'$ satisfy $$|\bm{s}-\bm{t}|\ll_U \frac{P^\varepsilon V_0 + L}{|\alpha P^2|},$$
by $A(\bm{y},\bm{v})$ applied with $1\leqslant j\leqslant \rho$,
together with the inequality \eqref{inverse-lipschitz-Psi}.
Then, \eqref{easy-grad-smooth} and
the case $\rho+1\leqslant j\leqslant n$ of $A(\bm{y},\bm{v})$
constrain the vector $\bm{v}''$ to lie in a box
$B(\bm{v}',\bm{y}'')$
of diameter
$$\ll_U \sup_{\bm{s},\bm{t}} |\alpha P^2| |\bm{s}-\bm{t}|
+ P^\varepsilon V_0 + L
\ll_U |\alpha P^2| \frac{P^\varepsilon V_0 + L}{|\alpha P^2|}
+ P^\varepsilon V_0 + L
\asymp P^\varepsilon V_0 + L.$$
The strategy is now to
choose $\bm{v}'$, $\bm{y}''$, $\bm{v}''$ and $\bm{y}'$ in that order,
where $$|\bm{v}'|\leqslant |\bm{v}|\leqslant |\bm{a}| + |\bm{v}-\bm{a}| \leqslant P^\varepsilon V + L.$$
Plugging \eqref{drop-L-box} into \eqref{choose-shifted box-max-vector-a}
and summing over $\bm{v}$,
it follows from our analysis of $\bm{v}'$ and $\bm{v}''$ above that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\sum_{\bm{v}\in \mathbb{Z}^n}
M_\alpha(\bm{v},L)
&\leqslant P^n \sum_{\bm{v}\in \mathbb{Z}^n} \int_{\substack{\bm{y}\in U\\
|\alpha P^2\Psi(\bm{y})-\bm{a}'|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0}}
\bm{1}_{|\bm{v}'| \leqslant P^\varepsilon V + L}
\bm{1}_{\bm{v}''\in B(\bm{v}',\bm{y}'')}\,
\mathrm{d}\bm{y} \\
&= P^n \sum_{\substack{\bm{v}'\in \mathbb{Z}^\rho\\ 
|\bm{v}'|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V + L}}
\int_{\substack{\bm{y}''\in \mathbb{R}^{n-\rho}\\ |\bm{y}''|\ll_U 1}}
\sum_{\bm{v}''\in B(\bm{v}',\bm{y}'')}
\int_{\substack{\bm{y}'\in \mathbb{R}^\rho\\ \bm{y}\in U\\
|\alpha P^2\Psi(\bm{y})-\bm{a}'|\leqslant P^\varepsilon V_0}}
\mathrm{d}\bm{y}'\, \mathrm{d}\bm{y}'',
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
by Fubini's theorem.
For any fixed $\bm{v}'$, $\bm{y}''$ and $\bm{v}''$, the inner volume is 
$$
\ll_U P^{O_n(\varepsilon)} \min\left\{1, \frac{ V_0}{R\phi P^2}\right\}^\rho,
$$
arguing via the diffeomorphism \eqref{key-diffeomorphism}
as in the proof of \eqref{preslop}.
The number of available vectors $\bm{v}'$ and $\bm{v}''$
being $O((1+P^\varepsilon V + L)^\rho)$ and $O((1+P^\varepsilon V_0 + L)^{n-\rho})$, respectively, we get
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{\bm{v}\in \mathbb{Z}^n}
M_\alpha(\bm{v},L)
\ll P^{n+O_n(\varepsilon)} (V + L)^\rho (1+V_0+L)^{n-\rho}
\min\left\{1, \frac{ V_0}{R\phi P^2}\right\}^\rho,
\end{equation*}
since $P^\varepsilon V\geqslant 1$.

If $\phi P^3\leqslant 1$ then $V=V_0=RP^{-1}$ and the overall bound is clearly
$O(P^{n+O_n(\varepsilon)} (V+L)^n)$,
since $P^\varepsilon V\geqslant 1$.
On the other hand, if 
 $\phi P^3>1$ then $V=R\phi P^2$ and
 $V_0=R\phi^{1/2}P^{1/2}$. But then
 $V_0/(R\phi P^2)=(\phi P^3)^{-1/2}< 1$, leading to the overall  contribution
$$
\ll P^{n+O_n(\varepsilon)} (V+L)^\rho (1+V_0+L)^{n-\rho} (V_0/V)^\rho
= P^{n+O_n(\varepsilon)} (1+\tfrac{L}{V})^\rho (1+V_0+L)^{n-\rho} V_0^\rho,
$$ 
as required.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- conjecture-2: body_md -->
\label{conj:clean-shifted}
Fix $n\geqslant 10$.
There exists a constant $b < 2n/3$ such that
for all real $\varepsilon>0$,
$B,L,R\geqslant 1/2$,
and vectors $\bm{v}\in \mathbb{Z}^n$ with $|\bm{v}|\leqslant B$,
we have
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{q\sim R} 
\sum_{\substack{\bm{0}\ne \bm{a}\in \mathbb{Z}^n\\ 
|\bm{a}-\bm{v}| \leqslant L}} |S_{q,W}(\bm{a})|
\ll_\varepsilon (BLR)^\varepsilon (L + R^{1/3})^n R^b.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end conjecture-2 -->
<!-- prop-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:remove-integral}
Assume Conjecture~\ref{conj:clean-shifted} for some fixed $n\geqslant 10$.
Let $\rho=r(F)$.
Then
\begin{equation*}
E(P;R,\phi) \ll \min\{1,\phi P^3\} \left(1 + P^{n-3+O(\eta+\varepsilon)-\Delta}\right),
\end{equation*}
where $\Delta = \min(\rho/4-3/2, \rho/2-1, 2n/3-b) > 0$ is admissible.
<!-- end prop-13 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
Plugging Lemma~\ref{aislop} with $\alpha = R\tau$
and Conjecture~\ref{conj:clean-shifted} with $B \ll P^{100}$
into \eqref{eq:bislop},
the desired bound is trivial unless
$P^\varepsilon V\geqslant 1$,
in which case
\begin{equation*}
E(P;R,\phi) \ll \phi + (1 + \tfrac{R^{1/3}}{L})^n \phi R^{b-n} P^{n+O_n(\varepsilon)}
\begin{cases}       
(1+\tfrac{L}{V})^\rho (V_0+L)^{n-\rho} V_0^\rho & \text{ if $\phi P^3>1$},\\
(V+L)^n & \text{ if $\phi P^3\leqslant 1$},
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
for any real $1\leqslant L\ll P^{100}$,
since $L\asymp \lceil{L}\rceil\in \mathbb{Z}$.
Here $1/2\leqslant R\ll P^{3/2}$ and $\phi \ll (RP^{3/2})^{-1+\eta}$.

If $\phi P^3\leqslant 1$ then $V=RP^{-1}$ and $P^\varepsilon V\gg 1$,
so $R^{1/3} \gg R/P = V \gg P^{-\varepsilon}$, since $R\ll P^{3/2}$.
Taking $L \asymp R^{1/3} \gg V$ gives
\begin{equation*}
E(P;R,\phi) \ll \phi + \phi R^{b - 2n/3} P^{n+O_n(\varepsilon)}
\ll \phi + \phi P^{b - 2n/3} P^{n+O(\varepsilon)},
\end{equation*}
since $R\gg P^{1-\varepsilon}$.
Thus $\Delta = 2n/3 - b > 0$ is admissible in this case.

Now suppose $\phi P^3>1$.
Then $V=R\phi P^2$ and
$V_0=R\phi^{1/2}P^{1/2}$,
with $P^\varepsilon V\gg 1$,
$V>V_0$
and $V_0 \ll (RP^{3/2})^{\eta/2} R^{1/2} P^{-1/4} \ll (RP^{3/2})^{\eta/2} R^{1/3}$.
Taking $L \asymp R^{1/3}$ gives
\begin{equation*}
E(P;R,\phi) \ll 1 + \phi R^{b-n} P^{n+O_n(\varepsilon)}  
(1+\tfrac{R^{1/3}}{V})^\rho (V_0+R^{1/3})^{n-\rho} V_0^\rho.
\end{equation*}
Writing $V = (\phi P^3)^{1/2}V_0$ and $V_0+R^{1/3} \ll (RP^{3/2})^{\eta/2} R^{1/3}$, this is
\begin{equation*}
\ll 1 + \phi R^{b-2n/3-\rho/3} P^{n+O(\eta+\varepsilon)}  
(V_0+\tfrac{R^{1/3}}{(\phi P^3)^{1/2}})^\rho.
\end{equation*}
Since $\rho\geqslant 2$, optimising over the interval $\max(P^{-3}, R^{-1} P^{-2-\varepsilon})
\ll \phi \ll (RP^{3/2})^{-1+\eta}$ gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
E(P;R,\phi) &\ll 1 + R^{b-2n/3-\rho/3} P^{n+O(\eta+\varepsilon)}  
(R^{-1}P^{-3/2} R^{\rho/2}P^{-\rho/4} + P^{-3} \max(1, P/R)^{1 - \rho/2} R^{\rho/3}) \\
&= 1 + R^{b-2n/3} P^{n-3+O(\eta+\varepsilon)}  
((R/P^{3/2})^{\rho/6 - 1} + \max(1, P/R)^{1 - \rho/2}).
\end{split}
\end{equation*}
By writing each term on the right-hand side as
$P$ raised to a piecewise linear function of the quantity $\log_P R$,
we find that this is optimised at either $R\asymp 1$, $R\asymp P$, or $R\asymp P^{3/2}$.
Thus
\begin{equation*}
E(P;R,\phi) \ll 1 + P^{n-3+O(\eta+\varepsilon)}  
((1/P^{3/2})^{\rho/6 - 1} + P^{1 - \rho/2} + P^{b-2n/3}).
\end{equation*}
Since $\rho = r(F)\geqslant \lceil 2n/3\rceil \geqslant 7$,
the saving $\Delta = \min(\rho/4-3/2, \rho/2-1, 2n/3-b) > 0$ is admissible.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{n10:ss}
There exist an integer $N\geqslant1$ and closed subschemes
\[
\operatorname{\mathbb{A}}^n_\mathbb{Z}=\mathcal Z_0\supset \mathcal Z_1\supset\cdots\supset \mathcal Z_n=\{\bm0\}
\]
defined by homogeneous polynomials such that the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \label{item:strat-geom-dim-bound}
We have $\dim (\mathcal Z_i \otimes \mathbb{Q}) \leqslant n-i$ for every $0\leqslant i\leqslant n$.

\item \label{item:strat-fourier-bound}
For every finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$
of characteristic $p\nmid N$, every $0\leqslant i\leqslant n-1$, and every
vector $\bm{v}\in \mathbb{F}_q^n \setminus \mathcal Z_{i+1}(\mathbb{F}_q)$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-bound}
T_q(\bm{v})\ll_{n,d} q^{(n-1+i)/2}.
\end{equation}

\item If $\mathcal X \otimes \mathbb{Q}$ is geometrically integral
and $d\geqslant 2$, then for every $0\leqslant i\leqslant n-1$, we have
\begin{equation}
\label{EQ:nice-sandwich}
\widehat W_i \subset \mathcal Z_{i+1} \otimes \mathbb{Q} \subset \widehat B_i,
\end{equation}
in the notation of \eqref{EQ:general-bad-hyperplanes}
and \eqref{EQ:general-large-gauss-fibres}.

\item Let $\overline{\mathcal Z_i(\mathbb{Q})}$ denote the Zariski closure of
$\mathcal Z_i(\mathbb{Q})$ in the variety $\mathcal Z_i \otimes \mathbb{Q}$.
If $\mathcal X(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$, then for every $1\leqslant i\leqslant n-1$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-main}
\dim \overline{\mathcal Z_i(\mathbb{Q})}
\leqslant n-i-1.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- rem-7: body_md -->
As in the main body of the paper,
we let $\widehat Y$ denote the affine cone of a projective variety $Y$,
where $\widehat \emptyset = \{\bm0\}$.
The reader may notice that \eqref{eq:main-bound} holds
trivially for all $\bm{v}\in \mathbb{F}_q^n$ if $i=n-1$, even if $\bm{v}\in \mathcal Z_n(\mathbb{F}_q)$.
Nonetheless, \eqref{EQ:nice-sandwich} for $i=n-1$ requires us to include the origin
$\bm0$ in $\mathcal Z_n$.
Including the origin
is also natural from the perspective of projective geometry,
which is pervasive throughout our paper.
<!-- end rem-7 -->
<!-- lemma-50: body_md -->
\label{app:ss:lem:homogeneity}
For every $\bm{v}\neq\bm0$, with $h=[\bm{v}]$, one has
\begin{equation*}
 T_q(\bm{v})=1+q\#X_h(k)-\#X(k).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-50 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
When $q=p$, this follows from
\eqref{eq:Sp-projective-v-nonzero}
together with the identity $S_p(\bm{v}) = pT_p(\bm{v})$
observed in \eqref{eq:pST}.
For general prime powers $q$, the same underlying algebraic manipulations apply.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- lemma-51: body_md -->
\label{app:ss:lem:reduction}
If $t\geqslant0$
and $G_h^i(\mathbb{Q}_\ell)$ is an isomorphism for all $i>t$, then,
for $\bm{v}\neq\bm0$ with $[\bm{v}]=h$,
\[
 T_q(\bm{v})\ll_{n,d} q^{t/2}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-51 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
In \eqref{app:ss:eq:trace}, the terms with $i>t$ vanish, since by assumption $G^i_h(\mathbb{Q}_\ell)$ is a Galois-equivariant isomorphism for $i>t$.
Deligne's general form of the Riemann hypothesis \cite[Th\'eor\`eme 3.3.1]{Del} bounds the
absolute values of the eigenvalues of the nonzero terms by
$q^{i/2}\leqslant q^{t/2}$.
Katz's bounds~\cite[Theorem~3 and its corollary]{KatzBetti}
bound the total Betti numbers of $X$ and $X_h$ in terms of $n,d$:
they are cut out by at most two equations of degree at most $d$.
The triangle inequality in \eqref{app:ss:eq:trace}
therefore gives the desired bound for $T_q(\bm{v})$.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- defin-4: body_md -->
\label{app:ss:def:Yi}
For $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$, define
\begin{equation}\label{app:ss:eq:Yi}
 Y_i=\{h\in P^\vee:\dim\Sigma_{\overline h}\geqslant i-1\},
\end{equation}
where $\overline h$ is a geometric point over $h$.
<!-- end defin-4 -->
<!-- lemma-52: body_md -->
\label{app:ss:lem:dimension}
The loci $Y_i$ satisfy $\operatorname{codim}_{P^\vee}Y_i\geqslant i$.
In particular $Y_n=\emptyset$.
<!-- end lemma-52 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
For an irreducible component
$E$ of $Y_i$ over an algebraic closure of $k$, a component of $\pi^{-1}(E)$
dominating $E$ has dimension at least $\dim E+i-1$. Hence
$\dim E+i-1\leqslant\dim\Sigma\leqslant n-2$, giving
$\dim E\leqslant n-1-i$. Thus $\operatorname{codim}_{P^\vee}Y_i\geqslant i$ and $Y_n=\emptyset$.
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- prop-14: body_md -->
\label{app:ss:prop:RS}
Let $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$.
For $h\notin Y_i$, the map $G_h^a(\Lambda)$
is an isomorphism if $a>n-2+i$, and is surjective if $a=n-2+i$.
<!-- end prop-14 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
We apply \cite[Theorem~1.2 and its proof]{RS} to
the inclusion morphism $\phi:X\hookrightarrow P$,
with parameters $r=\dim(X\times_P X)=\dim X=n-2$, $c=i$ and $q=a$.
The construction in \cite[Theorem~2.2, Corollary~2.3 and their proofs]{RS} chooses
precisely the loci $Y_i$ defined in \eqref{app:ss:eq:Yi}:
the cone of the morphism $i_h^*\mathcal F(-1)[-2]\to i_h^!\mathcal F$
defined in \eqref{EQ:derived-gysin-map}
is supported on
the image of $\Sigma_h$ in $H_h$.
Outside $Y_i$ this support has dimension at most $i-2$,
by the definition of $Y_i$.
The desired conclusion follows from the statement of \cite[Theorem~1.2]{RS},
with $Y_i$ in place of $Z_c$.
<!-- end proof-68 -->
<!-- lemma-53: body_md -->
\label{app:ss:lem:coefficients}
Fix a hyperplane $h$ and an integer $t$. Suppose $G_h^a(\mathbb{F}_\ell)$ is
an isomorphism for $a>t$ and is surjective for $a=t$. Then the same
statements hold with coefficients $\mathbb{Z}/\ell^r\mathbb{Z}$ for every $r\geqslant1$,
and with coefficients $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$ and $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$.
<!-- end lemma-53 -->
<!-- proof-69: body_md -->
Write $\Lambda_r=\mathbb{Z}/\ell^r\mathbb{Z}$ and abbreviate
\[
 A_r^a=H^{a-2}(X_{h,\overline k},\Lambda_r)(-1),\qquad
 B_r^a=H^a(X_{\overline k},\Lambda_r).
\]
For $r\geqslant2$, the coefficient sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow\Lambda_{r-1}\xrightarrow{\ell}\Lambda_r
       \longrightarrow\Lambda_1\longrightarrow0
\]
gives long exact sequences compatible with the Gysin maps,
by standard properties of derived tensor products with respect to distinguished triangles
in the derived category of $\Lambda_r$-modules.
To prove the statement of Lemma~\ref{app:ss:lem:coefficients} for $\mathbb{Z}/\ell^r\mathbb{Z}$,
we induct on $r\geqslant 1$.
The case $r=1$ is precisely our assumption,
so assume that $r\geqslant 2$ and the statement already holds for $r-1$.
For $a>t$, we obtain a commutative diagram that is exact on its horizontal arrows:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=small]
 A_1^{a-1}\arrow[r]\arrow[d]
 & A_{r-1}^{a}\arrow[r]\arrow[d]
 & A_r^a\arrow[r]\arrow[d]
 & A_1^a\arrow[r]\arrow[d]
 & A_{r-1}^{a+1}\arrow[d]\\
 B_1^{a-1}\arrow[r]
 & B_{r-1}^{a}\arrow[r]
 & B_r^a\arrow[r]
 & B_1^a\arrow[r]
 & B_{r-1}^{a+1}.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The first vertical map is surjective, and the second, fourth, and
fifth are isomorphisms. By the five lemma the middle map is thus an
isomorphism.
For $a=t$, the last four terms instead give surjectivity
of the middle map:
the maps on $A_{r-1}^t$ and $A_1^t$ are surjective,
and the map on $A_{r-1}^{t+1}$ is injective,
so the map on $A_r^t$ is surjective by the four lemma.

Since the finite-coefficient cohomology groups are finite, the inverse
systems of kernels of the surjective maps $G_h^t(\Lambda_r)$ satisfy
the Mittag--Leffler condition. Taking inverse limits therefore preserves
surjectivity at $a=t$, as well as the isomorphisms for $a>t$.
Now $H^b(Z,\mathbb{Z}_\ell)=\varprojlim_r H^b(Z,\Lambda_r)$,
                           
giving the assertions for $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$.
Finally, the identity
$H^b(Z,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=H^b(Z,\mathbb{Z}_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_\ell}\mathbb{Q}_\ell$
and the flatness of $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$ over $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$
lead to the result for $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$.
<!-- end proof-69 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{app:ss:cor:Ql}
Let $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$.
For $h\notin Y_i$, the map $G_h^a(\mathbb{Q}_\ell)$
is an isomorphism for $a>n-2+i$
and is surjective for $a=n-2+i$.
If $k=\mathbb{F}_q$ and
$\bm{v}\neq\bm0$ satisfies $[\bm{v}]\notin Y_i(k)$, then
$$T_q(\bm{v})\ll_{n,d} q^{(n-2+i)/2}.$$
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- proof-70: body_md -->
The first sentence follows from Lemma~\ref{app:ss:lem:coefficients} with $t=n-2+i$,
in view of Proposition~\ref{app:ss:prop:RS}.
We can use Lemma~\ref{app:ss:lem:reduction},
with $G_h^a(\mathbb{Q}_\ell)$ in place of $G_h^i(\mathbb{Q}_\ell)$,
to deduce the second sentence.
<!-- end proof-70 -->
<!-- prop-15: body_md -->
\label{app:ss:prop:global}
The schemes $\mathcal Z_i$ satisfy (\ref{item:strat-geom-dim-bound})
and (\ref{item:strat-fourier-bound}) of Theorem~\ref{n10:ss}.
<!-- end prop-15 -->
<!-- proof-71: body_md -->
The dimension assertions in (\ref{item:strat-geom-dim-bound})
have just been proved.
Suppose $p\nmid N$,
$0\leqslant i\leqslant n-1$, and $\bm{v}\notin \mathcal Z_{i+1}(\mathbb{F}_q)$.
Then $\bm{v}\neq\bm0$ and $[\bm{v}]\notin\mathcal Y_{i+1}(\mathbb{F}_q)$, so
Corollary~\ref{app:ss:cor:Ql} with $i+1$ in place of $i$
gives the required estimate for (\ref{item:strat-fourier-bound}),
since $\mathcal Y_{i+1}(\mathbb{F}_q) = Y_{i+1}(\mathbb{F}_q)$ by \eqref{app:ss:eq:relative-fibre}.
<!-- end proof-71 -->
<!-- lemma-54: body_md -->
\label{app:ss:lem:fibre-jump} 

Let $f:A\to B$ be a proper dominant morphism of integral varieties, and
put $c=\dim A-\dim B$. For $1\leqslant j\leqslant \dim B$, the closed locus
\[
 E_j=\{b\in B:\dim A_{\overline b}\geqslant c+j\}
\]
has codimension at least $j+1$ in $B$.
<!-- end lemma-54 -->
<!-- proof-72: body_md -->
This is trivial if $E_j=\emptyset$, so assume $E_j\ne \emptyset$.
The generic fibre dimension is $c$, so $E_j$ is a proper closed subset of $B$,
since $j\geqslant 1$.
Since $f$ is dominant, $f^{-1}(E_j)$ is a proper closed subset of $A$.
Since $A$ is integral,
$$\dim f^{-1}(E_j) \leqslant \dim A - 1 = \dim B + c-1.$$
However, for any irreducible component $E$ of $E_j$, some component of
$f^{-1}(E)$ dominating $E$ has dimension at least $\dim E+c+j$.
Thus $\dim f^{-1}(E_j) \geqslant \dim E_j+c+j$.
It follows that $\dim E_j \leqslant \dim B - j-1$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-72 -->
<!-- lemma-55: body_md -->
\label{app:ss:lem:dual-rational}
Let $V\subsetneq\operatorname{\mathbb{P}}^m_\mathbb{Q}$ be integral, but not necessarily geometrically
integral. If $V(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$, then
\[
 V^\vee(\mathbb{Q})\subset\operatorname{Sing}(V^\vee)(\mathbb{Q}).
\]
<!-- end lemma-55 -->
<!-- proof-73: body_md -->
Suppose that $h\in(V^\vee)_{\mathrm{sm}}(\mathbb{Q})$.
                                                                                                                                                             
The annihilator
\[
 (\mathbb T_hV^\vee)^\perp\subset\operatorname{\mathbb{P}}^m_\mathbb{Q}
\]
of the embedded tangent space is a projective linear space over $\mathbb{Q}$
of dimension $m-\dim V^\vee-1\geqslant0$. By biduality it is the fibre
over $h$ of $\mathcal N_V\to V^\vee$, viewed in the first factor,
and is therefore contained in $V$. It has a rational point,
contrary to the hypothesis $V(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$.
<!-- end proof-73 -->
<!-- prop-16: body_md -->
\label{app:ss:prop:rational-projective}
Assume $X(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$. For the generic-fibre loci
$Y_i=(\mathcal Y_i)_\mathbb{Q}$ and $1\leqslant i\leqslant n-1$,
\begin{equation*}
 \operatorname{codim}_{P^\vee_\mathbb{Q}}\overline{Y_i(\mathbb{Q})}\geqslant i+1.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end prop-16 -->
<!-- proof-74: body_md -->
The projection $\Sigma_\alpha\to V_\alpha^\vee$ has generic relative
dimension $c_\alpha=n-2-\dim V_\alpha^\vee$. Put
\[
 E_{\alpha,i}=\{h\in V_\alpha^\vee:
                       \dim(\Sigma_\alpha)_{\overline h}\geqslant i-1\}.
\]
Then $Y_i=\bigcup_\alpha E_{\alpha,i}$. We distinguish three cases.

If $c_\alpha>i-1$, then
$\dim V_\alpha^\vee=n-2-c_\alpha\leqslant n-i-2$, and the same bound
holds for $\overline{E_{\alpha,i}(\mathbb{Q})}$.

If $c_\alpha<i-1$, Lemma~\ref{app:ss:lem:fibre-jump} with
$1\leqslant j=i-1-c_\alpha\leqslant n-2-c_\alpha=\dim V_\alpha^\vee$ gives
\[
 \dim E_{\alpha,i}
 \leqslant\dim V_\alpha^\vee-(i-1-c_\alpha)-1=n-i-2.
\]

If $c_\alpha=i-1$, then $\dim V_\alpha^\vee=n-i-1$.
Since $V_\alpha\subset X$ has no rational point,
Lemma~\ref{app:ss:lem:dual-rational} implies that $V_\alpha^\vee(\mathbb{Q})$ lies in the proper
closed subset $\operatorname{Sing}(V_\alpha^\vee)$, of dimension at most $n-i-2$.
The closure of $E_{\alpha,i}(\mathbb{Q})$ satisfies the same bound.
<!-- end proof-74 -->
<!-- proof-75: body_md -->
Let $1\leqslant i\leqslant n-1$ and assume $X(\mathbb{Q})=\emptyset$.
Every nonzero $\mathbb{Q}$-point of $\mathcal Z_i$ projects to a $\mathbb{Q}$-point of $Y_i$.
Thus $\overline{\mathcal Z_i(\mathbb{Q})}$ lies in the affine cone over $\overline{Y_i(\mathbb{Q})}$,
so $\dim \overline{\mathcal Z_i(\mathbb{Q})} \leqslant 1 + \dim \overline{Y_i(\mathbb{Q})}
\leqslant n-i-1$ by Proposition~\ref{app:ss:prop:rational-projective}.
This proves \eqref{eq:rational-main}.
<!-- end proof-75 -->
